articles.title: Iran denies role in fridge hack, France summons ambassador
articles.summary: France has said it rules "nothing" out in response to a cyberattack on supermarket refrigeration units. Iran, however, said it categorically rejected Paris' "baseless and one-sided accusations" of…

image.caption: The apparent cyberattack forced hundreds of supermarkets to throw out spoiled produce after the refrigeration and freezer units went into a high-temperature defrost cycleImage: Elsa Rancel/Ouest-France/PHOTOPQR/MAXPPP/IMAGO

blocks.text: Iran on Tuesday dismissed French accusations that its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was behind a cyberattack on hundreds of supermarkets last month, as Paris summoned Tehran's ambassador to discuss the incident.

"Iran's Foreign Ministry categorically rejects the French government's baseless and one-sided accusations against Iran regarding alleged cyber activities in France," the ministry said, adding that it "strongly condemns this hackneyed policy of leveling accusations against the Islamic Republic."
The alleged attack, which began overnight on October 11-12, raised the temperatures in supermarket refrigerators and freezer units, spoiling produce and even causing fires in isolated instances.

A series of similar incidents have since followed in Europe and beyond, even including a failed attack on cooling units at French blood banks this month, though it is not yet clear if these subsequent events are connected.
France summons ambassador, says it rules 'nothing' out in response

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Tuesday that his government would "rule nothing out and will take all measures — including those we may not disclose publicly — that we deem proportionate and necessary to deter any further attacks."
Barrot was speaking amid a G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris that included discussions with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the conflict with Iran.

Barrot even said that despite a change in tone from the Trump administration since the midterm election defeat in the US, the risk of a renewed escalation with Iran could not be ruled out, "otherwise, we would not have devoted so much time and energy over the past two days to addressing these issues with our American counterpart."

blocks.caption: Barrot hosted G7 foreign ministers, including US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in Paris this weekImage: Brendan Smialowski/REUTERS

blocks.text: France summoned the Iranian ambassador on Tuesday and said it would be seeking European-level sanctions in response.
The EU said it would seek to provide a "swift and united response" pending discussion with member states.

"As the EU, we have consistently called on all states to refrain from malicious behavior in the cyberspace, and we will continue to address such malicious behavior, making use of all the tools that we have, also under the EU cyber diplomacy toolbox, including sanctions," spokesman Anouar El Anouni said.
Barrot said that the goal of any response would be "to deter anyone who might be tempted, in Iran or elsewhere, to do it again."
Iran accuses French of 'projecting' its own failures

Tehran appeared to threaten retaliatory measures of its own if sanctions materialized, saying it would "not hesitate to take necessary and appropriate measures to safeguard its national interests and security in the face of unlawful foreign activities."
It accused France of "merely projecting its own governance failures" with its allegations.
"A government that cannot even manage the temperature of its own refrigerators now seeks to shift the blame onto foreign actors through these preposterous accusations," it said.

blocks.caption: Around 700 supermarkets, of a total of roughly 10,000 across France, were affected by the alleged cyberattackImage: Stephane Mahe/REUTERS

blocks.text: What did Paris prosecutors say about suspected Iranian involvement?

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said on Monday that she had opened an investigation into leading members of Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit that is part of Iran's multi-force specialist military, the IRGC, that answers directly to its religious leadership.
She said her office had requested arrest warrants against two Shahid Kaveh officials and was investigating others.
She described the entity as "an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps."

French cyber intelligence agencies said the unit conducted "large-scale campaigns targeting industrial equipment for the purpose of sabotage." It said it primarily targeted Israel and the US, but also France and other European countries.

Beccuau said that the attack targeted roughly 700 of France's roughly 10,000 supermarkets. It used web interfaces to "initiate abnormal, indefinite defrost cycles," and also to disable automated alerts from sensors designed to go off when temperatures exceeded certain levels.
Sweden's Civil Defense Minister Carl-Oskar Bohlin warned that more cyberattacks could be expected in the coming months, as AI tools make it easier to detect and exploit vulnerabilities.

He said that it was not yet possible to say if hacks targeted Swedish supermarkets last week were connected, not least because the type of sabotage would have "been easy to copy" after seeing the initial reports in October.

articles.title: Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?
articles.summary: Hitler once called Eastern Europe "Germany's India." A new exhibition examines the links between colonialism and Nazism, and the bitter debate over where comparisons illuminate history and where they…

image.caption: European colonial rule was marked by the ruthless exploitation of people and resources, often enforced through extreme violence [Pictured: Clearing of land by setting grass on fire during a German research expedition to Tendaguru in German East Africa, 1909-1913]Image: Archiv/Museum für Naturkunde

blocks.text: Racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: at first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring "like the English, we shall rule this empire with handful of men."

But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire, and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared, remains the subject of intense debate. This is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust. Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history.

blocks.caption: 'Murder for the very purpose of murder': The industrialized mass murder carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau had no direct precedent in colonial historyImage: Taiftin/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: "I do think this is nonsense," says Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposed to be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story.
From colonial brutality to Nazi rule

The exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers. The juxtaposition highlights the contrast between colonial violence and the industrialized mass murder of the Holocaust. Yet it also points to connections: whips were used in Nazi concentration camps, while Fascist Italy deployed chemical weapons against civilians and soldiers during its invasion of Ethiopia (then Abyssinia) in 1935-36.

blocks.caption: The extreme brutality of Fascist Italy's invasion of Ethiopia, including the use of chemical weapons, caused uproar around the world [Pictured: The bombing of the Ethiopian village of Dessye by Italian planes on December 9, 1935]Image: Topfoto/United Archives International/IMAGO

blocks.text: In the 1930s, anti-colonial thinkers from India to the Caribbean argued that colonialism and fascism were two sides of the same coin. "There is nothing new or original about the blustering exploits of Hitler and Mussolini," observed the Trinidadian journalist and Pan-Africanist George Padmore in 1938. "They have all been used before by the British in their efforts to obtain the subjection of less powerfully armed and more industrially backward people."

European colonial rule was marked by the ruthless exploitation of people and resources, often enforced through extreme violence. In "The Origins of Totalitarianism" (1951), German-American philosopher Hannah Arendt argued that colonial territories served as laboratories for racial ideologies and practices of domination that could be applied beyond the legal constraints of Europe. Arendt described how these later "boomeranged" back into Europe and helped shape totalitarian politics in distinct and unprecedented form.

blocks.caption: One of the most notorious symbols of King Leopold II's rule was the amputation of hands, inflicted on men, women and children who failed to meet rubber production quotas [Pictured: A Congolese child with an amputated hand, 1900]Image: United Archives/World History Archive/IMAGO

blocks.text: The Congo Free State, King Leopold II of Belgium's private colony from 1885 to 1908, became notorious for its extreme brutality, as colonial authorities used executions, amputations, and sexual violence to ensure rubber production quotas were met. Forced labor was central to Nazi rule, with millions of Poles, Ukrainians, Russians and others from the Soviet Union, and Jews, subjected to exploitation and "Vernichtung durch Arbeit" ("extermination through work"). Within a few years, the regime mobilized around 13 to 14 million forced laborers, a scale comparable to the transatlantic slave trade over more than three centuries. The Nazis sought to extract value from their victims at every stage, confiscating their property, exploiting their labor, and even harvesting gold teeth and hair from the dead.
Racism, antisemitism and extermination

While racism underpinned both colonial empires and Nazism, Malinowski says the goals were different. The colonial powers tended to present assimilation as a path to advancement, forcing colonized people to adopt European culture, serve imperial interests, and suggesting that a select, educated few could gain opportunities at elite institutions such as Oxford or Cambridge. "This is definitely not something that the Nazi regime is offering to Poles or to Russians or let alone to Jews," added Malinowski.

"In terms of violence, colonial violence was just as extreme as Nazi violence. But Nazi violence was annihilatory and exterminatory compared to colonial violence in the colonies," says Edward Kissi, a historian at the School of Interdisciplinary Global Studies at the University of South Florida. He points to the example of how, unlike European colonial powers in Africa, the Nazis pursued the elimination of Black-Germans or peoples of African descent in Germany through forced sterilization. "Even in racism, colonial color-based racism and colonial anti-Jewish sentiments were fundamentally different from what the Nazis pursued."

blocks.caption: From 1904 to 1908, German colonial rule in present-day Namibia culminated in the genocide of the Herero and Nama, in which tens of thousands died [Pictured:  Concentration camp for Herero and Nama in German South West Africa, 1905]Image: Sam-Cohen-Bibliothek/Scientific Society Swakopmund

blocks.text: On October 2, 1904, German General Lothar von Trotha issued the "Vernichtungsbefehl" ("extermination order") following the Herero uprising in German South West Africa (present-day Namibia). Historians generally attribute the order to a combination of racial ideology, a desire to terrorize the population into submission, and efforts to secure colonial control over land, labor, and resources. Between 1904 and 1908, an estimated 60,000 to 80,000 Herero (around 80% of the population) and 10,000 (around half the population) Nama died.

One area where the exhibition draws no direct parallel is the industrialized killing carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau. "Where the two things really diverge is the Holocaust and is the systematic mass murder of the European Jews and it's murder for the very purpose of murder," explains Malinowski. The deportation of around 1,800 Jews from the Greek islands of Rhodes and Kos in July 1944 illustrates how Nazi persecution often defied military or economic logic: even after the war was effectively lost, the community was transported to Auschwitz, where most were murdered immediately upon arrival.
The politics of historical comparison

The issue of the "singularity" of the Holocaust came to the fore during the 1980s "Historikerstreit" ("historians' dispute"). Historian Ernst Nolte argued that Nazism should be understood in the wider context of 20th-century political violence, and as a response to Bolshevik terror in particular. Critics accused him of downplaying German responsibility for Nazi crimes.

Since 2020, a renewed debate dubbed the "Historikerstreit 2.0" has focused on whether the Holocaust should be viewed as a unique reference point in German memory culture or be understood alongside the histories of colonialism, racism and empire. The dispute now is less about the legitimacy of comparison than about its implications.

blocks.caption: After being deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau in 1943, French artist David Olère depicted scenes he witnessed. Here, deportees arrive at a crematorium shortly before their murder [Pictured: David Olère, 'Vers la mort' ('On the Way to Death'), Paris, 1945]Image: Mémorial de la Shoah/Coll. David Olère

blocks.text: The mass murder of tens of thousands of the Herero and Nama during four years of German colonial rule is now regarded as the first genocide of the 20th-century. In 2016, Nama representatives walked out of talks after Germany's chief negotiator said what happened was "incomparable" to the Holocaust. The German government has since recognized the events as genocide "from today's perspective," but it has not yet accepted legal liability or agreed to pay formal reparations.
Rethinking Germany's culture of remembrance

Martinican intellectual Aimé Césaire argued in "Discourse on Colonialism" (1950) that Europe condemned under Nazism forms of violence it had long accepted in its colonies. The exhibition opens amid renewed debates over settler colonialism, the definition of genocide, and the meaning of "never again," sharpened by Nicaragua's case against Germany at the International Court of Justice over German support for Israel during the war in Gaza. These tensions are reflected in visitors' comments in the exhibition's epilogue, even though the exhibition itself does not address Israel or Palestine beyond a reference to Mohammed Amin al-Husseini, appointed Grand Mufti of Jerusalem in 1921.

Germany has unequivocally accepted responsibility for the Holocaust, which is front and center of the country's culture of remembrance. However, Kissi likens Germany's apparent reluctance to reckon with its colonial history to debates in the US over slavery, in Cambodia over the Khmer Rouge, and in Turkey over the Armenian genocide. According to him, Germany's contemporary identity cannot be fully understood without examining its colonial history and the ways the Nazis appropriated and transformed aspects of that legacy. "I think Germans and all other human-beings who have experienced violent pasts and difficult pasts should be very careful not to delink or dissociate those facts from their present," Kissi said. "These are historical patterns. It is better to deal with these historical patterns and discomforts than to just fight them and then say this has absolutely nothing to do with German national identity."
"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence" is on show at the German Historical Museum until April 11, 2027

articles.title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
articles.summary:
Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent

Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet…
articles.byline: Associated Press at the Rafah crossing

blocks.text: Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.

The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.
Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.

blocks.caption: Lewis Hamilton (in black) listens to an Egyptian Red Crescent official during a visit to a logistics centre in Al-Arish. Photograph: Mohammed Arafat/AP

blocks.text: Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.
Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.
At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.
Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.
The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.
The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

articles.title: US inflation rose 0.4% in October as price increases cooled and gas costs dipped
articles.summary:
New data comes after Republicans’ midterms losses – which were largely seen as a rebuke of the party over high prices

US inflation rose 0.4% from September to October, slightly above…

blocks.text: US inflation rose 0.4% from September to October, slightly above expectations but still a cooldown in price increases as the cost of gas dipped during the month.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not release the usual year-over-year inflation figure as part of the consumer price index (CPI), which measures the price of a basket of goods and services, as data was not collected in October 2025 during the government shutdown.

But the newest data shows that prices are still increasing at a moderate pace. Economists estimate that, if interpolating the data for October 2025, the topline inflation figure for October 2026 would have been 3.9%, according to Oxford Economics. That would have been the highest its been since May 2026, when inflation reached 4.2%, a three-year high.

Higher energy costs driven by the Iran war have been the main factor behind increased inflation. Energy prices continued to rise slightly in October, rising 0.7% after going up 5.2% in September. In September, the overall monthly change in CPI from August was 0.6%.

The new data comes after a midterm election that will give Democrats control of Congress, in what was largely seen as a rebuke of Republicans over high prices. In their postmortem of the midterms, Republicans, including JD Vance, have specifically pointed to frustration over increased gas prices as a reason why the party fared so poorly in the election.

Gas prices cooled slightly in October, dropping from an average of $4.41 a gallon at the beginning of the month to $4.22 a gallon, prices are still more than $1 a gallon higher than a year ago, according to AAA. On Monday, the average price for a gallon at the pump fell below $4 for the first time since July.

The cost of diesel, which is used to power trucks, farming equipment, buses and trains, is nearly $2.50 a gallon higher compared with prices last year but has also been going down since October. Gas prices have continued to drop.

In September, the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 and are expected to hike rates again at their next meeting in December. Higher interest rates slow the economy by making borrowing money more expensive, and can slow inflation. The Fed’s target inflation rate is 2%, which it considers a stable pace for price increases.
Growth in the labor market surpassed economists’ expectations in October, giving more room for the Fed to hike rates. The unemployment rate has been relatively steady, hovering just above 4%.

Because today’s inflation is so closely tied to energy prices, it’s unclear how much and how quickly a rate hike could ease prices. But the Fed’s chair, Kevin Warsh, said the central bank is dedicated to making sure price increases ease up.
“Our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden across the economy, and that inflation expectations remain as they are anchored,” Warsh said on 28 October.

Consumer sentiment increased slightly at the end of October as gas prices eased, according to the University of Michigan’s Survey of Consumers. At the same time, the US stock market was experiencing a dip as investors voiced skepticism over the influx of AI spending.

“While sentiment lifted for lower- and middle-wealth consumers, it fell 5% for those with the largest stock portfolios in the wake of ​a relatively ​turbulent period ⁠in stock markets,” said Joanne Hsu, the director of the Surveys of Consumers, in a statement. “Moreover, ​consumers’ comments revealed growing anxiety over ​a ⁠possible AI bubble.”

articles.title: Poland: Krakow shooting suspect 'fascinated' by Norwegian mass murder Anders Breivik, says justice minister
articles.summary: The 24-year old suspect was found to have read a significant amount of material about Breivik and other far-right figures. Speculation over his motives have prompted a bitter political feud in Warsaw.

image.caption: The suspect, now deceased, is suspected of radicalization and severe psychiatric issuesImage: Jakub Porzycki/REUTERS

blocks.text: Polish Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek issued an update on Tuesday concerning the case of a mass shooting in Krakow over the weekend.
Accused gunman Michal Oksinski was deeply interested in international far-right movements, Zurek said.
"Authorities have accessed the terrorist's computer. It is clear that he visited websites concerning Anders Breivik," the Norwegian neo-Nazi who killed 77 people in July 2011, the minister added.
Zurek said a search of Oksinski's home turned up a Gadsen flag, a banner dating back to the US Civil War that is now associated with American white nationalists.
Police also gathered evidence that he had recently bought 10 magazines for a semi-automatic rifle and 500 bullets.
"It is clear that this individual was preparing to take action," the justice minister said.
Krakow shooting suspect 'fascinated by far right'
What happened in the attack?
On Friday night, 24-year-old Oksinski is thought to have shot and killed his mother, father, sister and two family cats in the city of Ostrowiec.

The following day at around 3:00 p.m. local time, Oksinski is suspected of opening fire in Krakow's Main Market Square. Six people were killed — four Poles, one Austrian, and one UK national. Another 15 people were wounded.
After the attack in Krakow, authorities discovered the bodies of his family members in Ostrowiec.
Poland then observed two days of national mourning. Oksinski died of wounds sustained during his arrest at a local hospital on Monday.
Initial investigations have uncovered "very solid" evidence pointing to far-right radicalization and psychiatric issues as motives for the attacks, Zurek said.
However, Zurek and the centrist government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk has been accused by members of right-wing populist PiS party of lying about Oksinski's motives.

articles.title: Sara Duterte's P64,000 Davao payout not reflected in 2024 ITR, prosecution says
articles.summary: The P64,000 payout that Vice President Sara Duterte received from the Davao City government in 2023 for her services as city mayor was not reflected in her income tax return (ITR) for the following…

blocks.text: Published November 10, 2026 11:14pm

The P64,000 payout that Vice President Sara Duterte received from the Davao City government in 2023 for her services as city mayor was not reflected in her income tax return (ITR) for the following year, the House prosecution panel said Tuesday.

Private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia made the claim, citing Duterte’s 2024 ITR, which did not indicate any compensation received from either the Davao City government or the Office of the Vice President (OVP).

Divinagracia then asked defense witness and Davao City Accountant Vingelin Bajan to confirm that Duterte’s 2024 ITR did not include compensation from either office. However, Bajan declined to give an answer.
“I cannot answer, Attorney,” Bajan said.

Bajan submitted photocopies of payroll summaries and disbursement vouchers, among other documents, showing that the P64,194.72 salary differential paid to Duterte covered the periods January to December 2020 and January to December 2021.
Bajan, however, said the payout was made only in January 2023 because the supporting documents were completed only at that time.
She also said she no longer had the original copies because these had already been submitted to the Commission on Audit (COA).
Divinagracia then asked Bajan if she had documentary proof that the COA had received the payroll summaries.
Bajan replied that transmitting such documents to the COA was the practice.

Divinagracia pointed out that this was not what she had asked and pressed Bajan to confirm: “In short, you do not have proof that these original documents are already in the possession of COA. Is that correct?”
Bajan replied, “Yes, Ma'am. Hindi ko po nadala po.”
(I was not able to bring them.)

Meanwhile, Senator Raffy Tulfo and Senate impeachment court Presiding Officer Francis Escudero questioned the handwritten corrections on some of the disbursement vouchers submitted by Bajan. The documents originally indicated the period January to December 2022, but this was later changed to January to December 2020 and January to December 2021.

Asked why the corrections were countersigned by hand, Bajan said the changes were made after supporting documents showed that the payouts to Duterte, now the Vice President, covered the periods January to December 2020 and January to December 2021.
“It was corrected on December 30, 2022,” Bajan said.
Tulfo then asked whether the correction was made belatedly, noting that the Constitution prohibits the Vice President from receiving double compensation.
Bajan attributed the delay to the lengthy process of preparing the disbursement vouchers. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Neuer injury gives Urbig chance to shape Bayern and Germany future
articles.summary: Manuel Neuer's latest injury gives Jonas Urbig a run of games in Bayern's goal. Marc-André ter Stegen remains Germany’s No. 1, but Urbig now has a chance to strengthen his case for the future.

image.caption: Manuel Neuer asked to be subbed off on Saturday due to pain in his right footImage: Attila Ziga/Eibner-Pressefoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: It's no secret that getting playing time is important to the development of any professional footballer – especially if your aspiration is to become the first-choice goalkeeper for your country . For most national team coaches, only a keeper who is playing regularly for his club merits consideration.

Unsurprisingly, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is no exception. While he did give Urbig – the backup keeper at Bayern – two starts in his first international break as national team boss, for the upcoming UEFA Nations League matches against Serbia and the Netherlands, Marc-André ter Stegen remains the undisputed No. 1.
What could Neuer's injury change?

But when Klopp gave ter Stegen the nod, Urbig was still spending most of his time on the bench in Munich. But this is set to change after Bayern's recent Bundesliga win over Mainz. The 40-year-old Manuel Neuer asked to be subbed off just before halftime, complaining of severe pain in his right foot.
An examination revealed that Neuer has sustained a partial tendon tear in the foot.
"An injury never comes at the right time, but it's part of the game," Neuer wrote on Instagram.
"I've been through this before, and I'll get through this one too. From now on: full focus on recovery. Until then, I will support the boys on the pitch wherever I can."

A partial tendon tear usually results in a layoff of six to 12 weeks, depending on the severity of the injury. Given that Neuer's foot already has some pre-existing damage from previous injuries, his recovery could take even longer.

blocks.caption: Jonas Urbig replaced Manuel Neuer on Saturday and is expected to take over full time in the futureImage: Jürgen Kessler/Kessler-Sportfotografie/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The goalkeeper of the future

Although Urbig is now the de-facto first-choice keeper for Bayern, he will still have to bide his time in the national team as understudy to ter Stegen. However, there is a general consensus that someday, Urbig will also become Germany's No. 1. With Neuer's contract running out in the summer, the chance to truly make the Bayern goal his own appears likely in the not-too-distant future.

The match on Saturday was Neuer's 550th in the Bundesliga and he also became the oldest player in a league match in Bayern's history when he took the pitch aged 40 years and 225 days. In other words, he can't go on forever.
One of his most famous predecessors in the Bayern goal has already called on him to draw a line under his highly successful career.

"I would tell him: 'Call it a day, Manu!' You have given an incredible amount to football, you have won everything, and you don't have to prove anything to anyone anymore," Sepp Maier, a member of West Germany's 1974 World Cup winning team told Sport1.
At some point, the now 82-year-old Maier noted, there comes a moment "when your body no longer behaves the way you want it to. And even a Manuel Neuer cannot stave off that moment."

For now, with ter Stegen playing regularly and performing well for Ajax, Germany coach Klopp is under no pressure to make a change. However, the 34-year-old former Barcelona keeper has, like Neuer, become quite injury-prone in recent years. Whenever he's needed, Urbig will be more than happy to seize his opportunity.
This article was adapted from German.

articles.title: New statue in DC mocks Trump for ‘dodging’ Vietnam war draft over bone spurs
articles.summary:
Gilded statue titled The Foot Soldier was installed on the National Mall just two days before Veterans Day

A

blocks.text: A new statue mocking Donald Trump was installed on Washington’s National Mall on Monday, this time poking fun at bone spurs that the US president was diagnosed with, which allowed him to defer the Vietnam war draft.

Just two days before Veterans Day, the gilded statue – titled The Foot Soldier – appeared near the National Gallery of Art’s Sculpture Garden. Created by the Secret Handshake, a group of anonymous artists, the statue depicts Trump sitting down while rubbing his bare foot.

“We honor the service and sacrifice of our commander in chief, Donald J Trump. He’s a soldier in spirit who marched to the front lines of dodging the draft, armed with a perfect diagnosis of bone spurs,” a plaque on the statue reads.

blocks.caption: A statue mocking Donald Trump’s Vietnam war draft deferments due to a diagnosis of bone spurs is displayed on the National Mall in Washington DC on 9 November 2026. Photograph: Mehmet Eser/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: The art piece refers to allegations that Trump dodged the Vietnam war draft in 1968 by receiving a diagnosis of bone spurs in his heels after he graduated from college.

“We salute a leader who knows you can’t spell sacrifice without ‘I,’ and a warrior who reminds us that sometimes when you’re called to stand up, it’s best to just sit down and rest your feet,” the plaque read.
“Toey”, a 6ft-tall mascot of a toe suffering from bone spurs, stood next to the art installation serving as an interactive element, the Secret Handshake said in a statement.
“Draft dodger? I hardly know her,” a person dressed as Toey told the Washington Post. “I’m the biggest toe. The hugest toe. Huge. Hugest toe. Largest toe that anyone’s ever seen.”

Trump has faced draft-dodging allegations since his first term. In 2018, the New York Times published an article accusing a foot doctor in Queens of doing “a favor” for Trump’s father by diagnosing Trump with bone spurs. In 2019, Michael Cohen, a former lawyer for Trump, told Congress that the president deliberately avoided the draft.

blocks.caption: A statue mocking Donald Trump’s Vietnam war draft deferments due to a diagnosis of bone spurs is displayed on the National Mall in Washington DC on 9 November 2026. Photograph: Mehmet Eser/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: David Ingle, a spokesperson for the White House, said in a statement,: “Trump Derangement Syndrome is a sick and incurable disease that has rotted the brains of these Democrat activists. President Trump will never waver in fighting for and protecting the American people.”
The Secret Handshake has also erected statues making fun of Trump’s relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and Trump’s remodeling of the Lincoln bathroom during a government shutdown.

Last year, the anonymous group of artists created Best Friends Forever, a statue that showed Trump holding hands with Epstein. In March, the Secret Handshake installed a statue called King of the World, which depicted Trump holding Epstein in a Titanic-inspired pose.
The Foot Soldier and Toey will be at the National Mall through Veterans Day, the Secret Handshake said.

articles.title: Jimmy Carter’s Georgia farm to open to the public: ‘This land shaped him and his legacy’
articles.summary:
Conservation group acquires former US president’s family farm with plans to transfer it to the state in 2028

Jimmy Carter’s…

blocks.text: Jimmy Carter’s family farm has been acquired by a group dedicated to permanently protecting the south-west Georgia land where the late former president’s conservation ethic took hold, officials announced on Monday.

A statement from the Conservation Fund said it plans to open Carter’s family farm – on about 2,458 acres (995 hectares) outside his home town of Plains, Georgia – to the public for hunting, fishing and other outdoor recreation as soon as 2027, with the group set to transfer the land to the state’s natural resources department in 2028.

Plans call for the Carter family farm to ultimately become part of Georgia’s Lanahassee Creek wildlife management area, expanding it to nearly 7,000 acres (2,833 hectares), according to the Conservation Fund.

The non-profit organization also said its purchase of the Carter family farm ensures the protection of a property that was dear to the man who served as US president for four years beginning in 1977 – and later won a Nobel peace prize for his humanitarian work.

After being raised on his family’s farm, Carter signed the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act in late 1980, protecting more than 104m acres in what remains the US’s largest protected public lands expansion in US history, the Conservation Fund said.
He also established 39 national park system units, among them the Martin Luther King Jr national historic site and the Chattahoochee River national recreation area in Georgia’s capital city, Atlanta.

The Conservation Fund traced a direct link between those accomplishments and Carter’s upbringing on the farm where he worked alongside his father, Earl, in their family’s peanut, corn and sugarcane growing operations. He also explored the surrounding woods and returned to the land that the Carter family bought in the early 1900s throughout his life – to hunt; walk with his late wife, Rosalynn; and fish in the property’s pond, including toward the end of the couple’s lives.

Carter successfully requested that his family maintain a stand of mature longleaf pine trees, according to the Conservation Fund. And in one of his final land conservation decisions, the group said, Carter had much of the farm replanted with young longleaf pine.

That move aimed to help restore the native forest once covering the region, a vital habit for tortoises, which conservationists have been working to keep from becoming an endangered species. Creeks adjacent to the Carter family farm are also home to freshwater mussels, which are rare.

“Long before Jimmy Carter protected millions of acres across America, he was a boy working the fields and roaming the woods of southwest Georgia,” said a statement attributed to Stacy Funderburke, vice-president of the Conservation Fund’s central south-east region. “This land shaped him and his legacy, and he never stopped coming home to it.
“We’re honored to help ensure this land remains a healthy habitat for wildlife, and we look forward to the day it is open to everyone who wants to experience it.”

The former president’s grandson, Jason, said in a separate statement: “For our family, this land was always about more than a farm. It was home – a place my grandparents treasured. We’re grateful to The Conservation Fund and to everyone working to make sure it’s protected for generations to come.”

The Conservation Fund said the Carter family farm is distinct from his boyhood home, which is maintained by the US national park service and preserves the house where the former president lived as a child.

A former governor of Georgia, Carter – a Democrat – defeated incumbent Republican president Gerald Ford to clinch his lone Oval Office term. He then lost the presidency to Republican challenger Ronald Reagan during the 1980 election amid the Iran hostage crisis.

After his presidency, Carter won the 2002 Nobel peace prize for his work seeking peaceful resolutions to global conflicts, advancing human rights and democracy, and promoting economic and social development.
The devout Baptist died aged 100 in December 2024, a little more than a year after the death of Rosalynn Carter, his wife.

articles.title: The vaccine limbo in the US is worsening the measles outbreak
articles.summary:
Earlier doses for children, a focus on unvaccinated adults, a risk strategy based on geography – here’s how a functioning ACIP would address the measles outbreak

The US has announced three…

blocks.text: The US has announced three deaths associated with measles last week, among them a seven-month-old baby in New York and a postpartum woman in Pennsylvania, underscoring the need for a more aggressive vaccination approach – but US recommendations haven’t changed.

Dismantling the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) made it harder for the US to respond to the measles outbreak, with vaccine recommendations staying the same during a historic rise in cases and deaths, four former advisers say.

A functioning committee would likely be considering recommendations on reaching adults with vaccines; moving up the childhood schedule for measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination in stricken areas; and pinpointing exactly which groups and areas need vaccination campaigns, they said.

Months after Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), replaced vaccine advisers with his own handpicked allies, a federal judge halted the committee’s work, finding that the Trump administration had failed to constitute the committee properly.

The ACIP makes recommendations to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on vaccine policy – and it “definitely” would discuss updating its advice as measles continues to spread, said Yvonne “Bonnie” Maldonado, chief of infectious diseases in the department of pediatrics at Stanford Medicine and a former member of the ACIP.
Now, “we don’t have an ACIP”, Maldonado added. “That’s going to impact disease and deaths in the US.”

The committee was monitoring the measles outbreak early last year before Kennedy disbanded it, and his replacements did not publicly evaluate evidence on the outbreak. The CDC is now taking nominations for a new committee, but the appointment process can take months or years – and the process for making or changing recommendations is also lengthy.

“It typically took between 12 to 18 months from the start of considering new recommendations to adopting them,” said Noel Brewer, a distinguished professor of health behavior at the UNC Gillings School of Global Public Health and a former ACIP member. In the meantime, the outbreak continues accelerating.

The seven-month-old baby who died in New York state wasn’t vaccinated against measles, officials said on Monday. Another infant died in the measles outbreak in Wisconsin, officials announced on Thursday. Both states marked their first measles-associated deaths in three decades.

In normal times, babies in the US don’t receive their first MMR shots until they turn one. But during outbreaks, babies at risk of infection can get the shot as early as six months of age – one of a handful of recommendations from the CDC that is receiving less attention than it normally would, experts say.

The advice on vaccination during outbreaks could be highlighted more, and recommendations could be changed to “tell the pediatricians and providers we are in a huge outbreak”, said Edwin Asturias, professor of pediatric infectious disease at the University of Colorado and a former ACIP member.

The CDC also offers the option of moving up the MMR second shot in order to make sure children in outbreak areas are fully protected against the virus. During an outbreak, it can be given as soon as four weeks after the first dose. The shot is usually given between the ages of four and six.
The delay between doses could be contributing to what Asturias calls a “group of susceptibles” who were not protected from measles for decades and are now falling ill and dying.

Some people are ideologically opposed to vaccines, while others don’t have steady access to healthcare. “But that’s only part of the explanation,” Asturias said. The number of visits to doctors decreases dramatically after the second year of life, with fewer opportunities to get the shots. “By delaying the second dose of immunization to four to six years, are you more likely to miss or not to give a second dose to many children?” he asked.
A properly appointed ACIP would look at such data points to “try to understand how this immunization or protection gap came about”, Asturias said.

In the US, vaccine mandates for children are set at the state and local level, tied to daycare and school attendance. But moving the recommendation earlier might increase vaccination rates, since families tend to have higher levels of trust in their doctors than in local officials, for example.
An unusually high number of adolescents and young adults are now getting sick and dying from measles. The vaccine advisers would likely explore why, and what could be done to reach them.

“Are you really monitoring how many adults are getting infected? I doubt it,” said Paul Offit, an infectious diseases physician at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia and a member of the ACIP two decades ago. “Are we trying to vaccinate them? It’s harder. You can have school mandates, but what do you do for adults?”

It is especially important to reach unvaccinated or under-vaccinated people before they become pregnant, because the vaccines cannot be given during pregnancy. Congenital measles cases – when a baby gets sick in utero – have risen sharply this year, officials in Pennsylvania warned recently.

Such infections threaten the lives of newborns and pregnant people alike. A 21-year-old woman in Pennsylvania died soon after childbirth from measles complications, officials announced this week. Earlier this year, a measles-infected baby died soon after birth.

“That’s the actual heart of the situation,” Maldonado said. “What we’re seeing now is something I literally have never seen myself, and I’m a seasoned infectious disease clinician,” she added. “To have even one case used to be a remarkable occurrence, but now they’re having so many.”

Anyone beginning cancer therapy or other immune-suppressing treatments should also make sure they’re protected by vaccines first, Asturias said. And anyone who was born between 1968 and 1989 may have only received one shot, and should get a second dose.
The ACIP should also work to identify which groups of people and regions are most at risk and how to reach them, said Brewer.

“Measles vaccination rates are pretty high in most places, but there are places where it’s very low, and the United States does not have a good mechanism for identifying these geographical areas and responding in them,” Brewer said.

The ACIP and the CDC offer recommendations based on evidence that is sometimes not publicly available. But states can take action on their own to change vaccination recommendations. “The decisions are up to the states and the counties,” Maldonado said.

With measles, “there are serious risks” and “most of the bad stuff happens to young babies under a year of age”, Maldonado said. Hospitalizations, complications and deaths are more common in this group – and the risks persist long after the rash fades. Maldonado has cared for two children who developed subacute sclerosing panencephalitis years after contracting measles.
“They’re terrifying cases,” she said.

Yet US officials have lagged in public communications about the risks – and how preventable they are, Maldonado said. Erica Schwartz, the CDC’s director, drew criticism for her silence on the outbreaks and the importance of vaccination.

“She came into CDC in the middle of a huge set of outbreaks and didn’t talk about it for weeks,” Maldonado said. For families seeking guidance, “it’s already pretty chaotic right now, and it’s unfortunate – nobody knows where to turn”, Maldonado said.

US officials need to speak with “one voice” to outline a plan for addressing the outbreak, Brewer said. “The US has a terrible measles problem right now, one that is largely avoidable. We need to get vaccination rates up.”
He added: “That’s really the key priority: just get the shot.”

articles.title: Police receive further criminal allegations against Russell Brand
articles.summary: Met says several people have been in contact since start of disgraced comedian’s rape and sexual assault trial
articles.byline: Jessica Elgot, Michael Savage and Emine Sinmaz

blocks.text: Police have received further criminal allegations against Russell Brand since the start of his trial.
The Metropolitan police said several people had been in contact during and since the conclusion of the 51-year-old’s rape and sexual assault case.
The force said those who had been in contact had either provided further information or reported potential criminal allegations.

A spokesperson said: “Several people have contacted the investigation team during and since the trial to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation. Detectives are assessing this information as part of their ongoing inquiries.”
The judge in Brand’s trial, Mr Justice Bennathan, praised the bravery of the women who had come forward with evidence that led to his conviction.
But the way the victims were questioned by the disgraced comedian’s legal representative, Ian Winter KC, has been criticised in recent days.
Labour’s deputy leader, Lucy Powell, described the cross-examination as “depressing”, saying she believed the courts had “long gone past that sort of culture”.
Powell, who is also the education secretary, said that she regretted a meeting the former party leader Ed Miliband had with Brand in 2015 when she was Labour’s campaign chief.
Brand was jailed for 10 and a half years on Monday for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others, including at their workplaces.

Powell was asked on LBC radio about Brand’s defence in court, during which Winter suggested he must be innocent because none of his victims had “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”. Winter also said the anal rape of a 21-year-old woman was a “short and momentary failure” where “he did not respect her consent”.

blocks.caption: Ian Winter KC leaves Southwark crown court after Russell Brand’s sentencing.  Photograph: Tayfun Salci

blocks.text: Asked if that was reminiscent of the attitude of the 1950s, Powell said she had been shocked at some of what took place in the courtroom, while praising the judge’s words. “I found reading some of that incredibly sort of depressing. I thought we’d long gone past that sort of culture and that phase of things.

“And the judge’s remarks were also incredibly powerful in sentencing: that it doesn’t matter what you wear, how you behaved, how drunk you are, you know, you have the right to give your consent or not give your consent. And if it’s not given, then that is rape and that is a sexual offence, pure and simple.”

The BBC’s director general, Matt Brittin, wrote to the corporation’s staff to say that he wanted to ensure any concerns raised about workplace culture were heard “at the highest level”. His intervention followed criticism that Brand’s troubling behaviour had not been challenged properly during his time at the broadcaster.
Brittin said in his email that there had been valid criticism levelled at the media industry over its workplace culture after Brand’s conviction and recent allegations of antisemitism at the BBC.

Brand, who had stints as a presenter on BBC 6 Music and Radio 2 in 2006 and 2007, once joked on air about exposing himself to a woman moments before his show was broadcast. He also described one BBC boss, who has since left the broadcaster, as “incredibly tolerant” of his behaviour.

Brittin said the BBC and the wider media industry had made progress in improving culture, but that there was “still more to do to engage with staff and represent their views and concerns at the highest level”.
after newsletter promotion
Brittin said he was looking at changes to improve culture that could be made immediately and as part of the next BBC charter being discussed with ministers.
The BBC published a review in 2025 that found some staff had felt unable to speak out because of Brand’s status and power. The corporation repeated its apology this week.

After the treatment of some of Brand’s accusers during his trial, Powell said the government had taken steps in guidance to challenge myths about rape and victim-blaming in court. “But clearly, a lot more needs to be done because I think many of us were really shocked that that could still take place in a courtroom today,” she said.

blocks.caption: Lucy Powell said a lot more needed to be done to challenge myths around rape and victim-blaming in court. Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PA

blocks.text: At sentencing, the judge criticised Brand, saying the women had been subjected to additional suffering because of the conduct in court “on your instructions”.

“Whatever women wear, wherever they go, whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and demand justice in the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Mr Brand, act without their consent,” he said.

Powell said she and Miliband regretted that he had done an interview with Brand in 2015 during the hype around Revolution, Brand’s book on politics. At the time the interview took place, Brand had resigned from his BBC Radio 2 show for leaving a series of lewd messages on actor Andrew Sachs’ answerphone about his granddaughter.

“It was a long time ago, obviously, and had I or Ed Miliband or anybody at the time had any sense at all that this was someone who was a sexual predator, who was involved in these sorts of crimes,” she told Sky News, anyone who was involved in promoting him would “look back and really regret that, knowing today what we now know”.

Asked about her role in setting up the interview, Powell said she had not understood the full extent of his sexual conduct that was already in the public domain – such as in his autobiography. “If there was any suggestion at all we were dealing with someone who was a known sexual predator at the time then, of course, no one would have done that.
“But as I say, he was a well-known public figure. Lots of people, from Hollywood to the BBC to many others, gave this person a very, very powerful platform.”

The falling star of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang | About That

Nvidia announced ⁠a probe into the matter on Sunday. Its shares closed ⁠down ⁠4.3 per cent on Monday, reducing Nvidia's market capitalization by approximately $190 billion US. The lawsuit was filed five minutes after ⁠the U.S. stock market closed.

articles.title: UK and Argentina clash over Falklands oil project as Hamburg tribunal starts
articles.summary:
Sea Lion project in the North Falkland basin threatens to deepen sovereignty dispute

Argentina has told an international tribunal that Britain’s approval of oil drilling off the Falkland…

blocks.text: Argentina has told an international tribunal that Britain’s approval of oil drilling off the Falkland Islands has dramatically deepened a sovereignty dispute that led to war four decades ago.
At the start of an historic legal clash at the Hamburg-based International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (Itlos), an Argentinian legal team argued that the oil project must be suspended.

Javier Oyarzábal, chief legal adviser to Argentina’s ministry of foreign affairs, said that the 3,400 inhabitants of the Falkland Islands, whose status as a British overseas territory is disputed by Buenos Aires, had no right to the resources around the south Atlantic archipelago.

Oyarzábal said: “[Argentina] respects the interests of the inhabitants of the islands and their way of life as enshrined in the Argentine constitution … What these British citizens do not have is a right to decide to which state the islands belong …
“These resources belong to the Argentine people. Some 46 million of them including the 1,247 inhabitants born on the islands whose interests will be duly taken into account.”

Oyarzábal said Argentina was ready to negotiate “all aspects of the question” of the Falkland Islands, which are known as the Malvinas in Argentina, “including the present aggravation of the dispute caused by the UK”.
He accused the UK of refusing to enter talks over the islands while pushing forward on the exploitation of its natural resources in a way that would entrench the status quo.
Oyarzábal claimed that the oil money from the drilling would “finance the very military base and presence that sustains the UK’s de facto control of the territory”.

Addressing the panel’s chair, Judge Maurice Kamga, from Cameroon, he added: “Mr President, the UK cannot have it both ways. It cannot invoke the sovereignty dispute to escape jurisdiction [of Itlos] while exploiting the natural resources of the disputed area as if a dispute had already been resolved in its favour.”
The Sea Lion project in the North Falkland basin, led by the Israeli-firm Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper, has the potential to triple the islands’ GDP per capita.

It has been condemned as unlawful by Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, and his government has applied for arbitration by Itlos over the future of the project, claiming Britain’s approval of is in breach of a 1976 UN resolution calling on both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands until the sovereignty dispute is settled.

Argentina is requesting urgent provisional measures, including a commitment from the UK to “stop the drilling” which, Oyarzábal said would do no more than “preserve the present situation” and allow for constructive talks over sovereignty to begin.

At the start of the two-day hearing, the tribunal’s panel was told that a decision by the UK government to allow drilling to start in March next year was the “unilateral conduct” of a “colonial power”.

It was further claimed by Argentina that the Sea Lion oil project risked an environmental disaster on Argentina’s doorstep and that it would make the sovereignty dispute over the islands “more difficult or impossible” to resolve peacefully.

He added: “In the event of a blowout or spill, it is Argentina that would bear its consequences and be called upon to respond, not a state that is 12,700km away. More over the project lies within the search and rescue region for which Argentina is responsible”.

The long-standing dispute between Argentina and the UK over the sovereignty of the Falklands led to war in 1982 at the cost of the lives of 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders.
The hearing is the first time that substantive matters relating to the Falklands have been litigated at an international tribunal.

The oil project is seen on the islands as offering the opportunity to secure their economic future, and build a sovereign wealth fund, at a time when fisheries catches on which they depend are declining.
In a show of solidarity, Princess Anne arrived in Port Stanley on Monday. Ellie Reeves, the UK’s attorney general, attended the Itlos hearing on Tuesday.

She claimed that Argentina was seeking to litigate the issue of sovereignty through Itlos, an independent judicial body established by the 1982 United Nations convention on the law of the sea to oversee maritime disputes.
She said: “We don’t think this is the forum to effectively determine sovereignty issues.”

Asked whether the UK would abide by any ruling, Reeves said: “We don’t know what’s going to happen in terms of the outcome but we don’t consider they have jurisdiction on sovereignty issues. We respect the court and the institutions … but I don’t want to get ahead of what the tribunal may or may not say.” The hearing continues.

articles.title: Defiant Hegseth calls Republican's impeachment resolution a 'farce'
articles.summary: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth condemned a resolution in the House of Representatives calling for his impeachment, describing it as a "farce" from a "disgruntled congressman" who is leaving…

image.caption: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth speaks during a press conference at the Pentagon in Washington on Tuesday. (Nathan Howard/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth condemned a resolution in the House of Representatives calling for his impeachment, describing it as a "farce" from a "disgruntled congressman" who is leaving office.
Next steps after Rep. Thomas Massie's impeachment bid still unclear
Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie, who won't be in Congress when the new session begins in January, filed a privileged motion on the House floor on Monday to introduce eight articles of impeachment.

Impeachment resolutions can carry over to the next session, which begins on Jan. 3 and will feature a House and Senate led by the Democrats. A two-thirds majority of the Senate vote is required for conviction.

Hegseth said any such proceeding would be a "show trial against the president and the secretary of war" and he characterized the articles of impeachment as "policy disagreements" that don't meet the impeachment standard of high crimes and misdemeanours.
"The proper remedy for a policy disagreement, it's legislation, it's debate, it's the next presidential election," said Hegseth, holding his first press briefing from the Pentagon since May.
U.S. House Republican moves to force vote on impeaching Pete Hegseth

President Donald Trump gave an enthusiastic response on social media to Hegseth's pushback. Trump on Monday called Massie a "stone-cold loser" and said he would stand by Hegseth even if he is impeached.

Under the rules of Massie's motion, a vote is to be held within two legislative days unless a majority supports a countering motion to kill the effort. Massie introduced a similar measure in September but the House legislators were sent home before a vote could take place.
A vote in the House could come by midweek, but the next steps are highly uncertain.
'They will fail again'

The articles of impeachment in Massie's motion lead with the lack of congressional authorization for the war in Iran. The articles also include references to Hegseth's role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela, the deadly strikes on boats allegedly transporting drugs in waters near South America and attempts to prosecute two Congress members who served in the military and recording a video advising service members they were not obliged to follow illegal orders.
"I stand behind every one of these operations," Hegseth said on Tuesday.

He said "thousands of American lives" were saved with every boat strike — even as human rights organizations and international bodies have said they possibly constitute crimes against humanity. Hegseth also said that former Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro was "not kidnapped, he was brought to justice by America's best."
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky speaks Monday outside the Capitol about articles of impeachment against Hegseth. (Allison Robbert/The Associated Press)
Massie, who was defeated earlier this year by a Trump-backed Republican opponent in a primary, pushed forward an impeachment resolution over the objections of House Republican leadership.

"The reality is, we're not indicting him for being bad at his job," Massie told reporters on Monday. "In fact, he was very effective at killing school children in Iran. He was very effective at extrajudicial killings."
Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson has said a vote on impeachment would be "a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see."
Democrat Hakeem Jeffries, Johnson's potential successor as the next Speaker, said on the weekend he was a "hard yes" for impeaching Hegseth.

items: Several U.S. military bases, diplomatic buildings have been damaged in Iran war: inspector general report
UN mission finds 'grounds to believe' U.S. committed war crimes in strikes on Iranian school, sports centre

blocks.text: The last House impeachment was of former Homeland Security chief Alejandro Mayorkas in Joe Biden's administration, for breach of public trust and willful refusal to comply with the law. The Republican-led House cited the surge of migrants at the southern border in just the second impeachment of a cabinet secretary, but the Democratic-led Senate never took up the measure.

Trump was twice impeached in the House, in 2019 and 2021, but acquitted at Senate trials. In the second impeachment, many Republicans argued that Trump's actions leading up to the 2021 Capitol riot were best dealt with in the courts, a stance that unintentionally saw Trump fundraise and launch a remarkable political comeback to return to the White House.
Hegseth called those Trump impeachments failures and predicted that the current efforts "will fail again."
Razor-thin confirmation

A vote will put pressure on Republicans, many of whom blamed their election wipeout on the Iran war. Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska highlighted other concerns not contained in the articles, concerning Hegseth's firing of dozens of senior military leaders.

Vice-President JD Vance broke a tie in the Senate to enable Hegseth's confirmation in early 2025. Republicans Susan Collins and Mitch McConnell — each set to leave Congress — voted against his confirmation, as did Republican Lisa Murkowski and all of the Senate Democrats.
Thom Tillis, a Republican also leaving the Senate, has expressed regret for his vote to confirm Hegseth.

"He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defence and the health and well-being of our fighting force," Tillis said of Hegseth in September.
LISTEN | David Smith, Washington reporter for the Guardian, on Hegseth's influence (March 16):
Front Burner30:05Pete Hegseth: the Iran war’s chief promoter

A number of episodes sparked concern about Hegseth's fitness for the job among Democratic lawmakers and the handful of Republicans, including a 2017 sexual assault allegation. Hegseth admitted paying a settlement to the woman, to prevent a costly and drawn-out process.
Other accusations that arose during his confirmation hearings involved excessive drinking and financial mismanagement at two veterans' organizations he previously led.

During Trump's first term, Hegseth was an on-air Fox News contributor who lobbied the president on behalf of Navy Seal Eddie Gallagher, Maj. Matthew Golsteyn and Lt. Clint Lorance before military tribunals involving the men had even been completed. Each man had faced accusations of war crimes, but Hegseth argued they were being treated unfairly.

items: Trump, Hegseth declare end to 'woke' culture in politicized speech to service members

blocks.text: Trump ultimately granted clemency to Golsteyn and Lorance, and elevated Gallagher in rank.

Hegseth's tenure at the Pentagon has been unconventional, and that was on display on Tuesday. Defence secretaries typically stay away from partisan political statements, but Hegseth laid out criticisms of predecessor Lloyd Austin and disparaged the military recruitment and retention efforts of Biden's administration.
He also told the U.S. troops to "stay the course" while evoking his Christianity, even as he has been sued for imposing his religion on federal workers.

Chris Iorfida, based in Toronto, has been with CBC since 2002 and written on subjects as diverse as politics, business, health, sports, arts and entertainment, science and technology.

articles.title: Prosecution seeks sanctions vs. VP Sara, spokesperson over alleged sub judice violations
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel has asked the Senate impeachment court to sanction Vice President Sara Duterte and her spokesperson, Atty. Paolo Panelo, over statements that allegedly violated the sub…

blocks.text: Published November 10, 2026 10:41pm

The House prosecution panel has asked the Senate impeachment court to sanction Vice President Sara Duterte and her spokesperson, Atty. Paolo Panelo, over statements that allegedly violated the sub judice rule, including remarks that supposedly questioned the integrity of the court.

Private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa Jr. made the call on Tuesday after lead defense counsel Sheila Sison urged the court to take action over Tolosa’s statements, which she claimed delved into the merits of the impeachment case against the Vice President in violation of the sub judice rule.
Senate impeachment court Presiding Officer Francis Escudero said the court had been looking into statements made by both parties over the weekend that may have violated the sub judice rule.

“We've heard that from the Vice President time and again, as well as her spokesperson attacking their integrity, attacking their motives, saying the impeachment proceedings have been marred by bending the law, saying that senators are manipulating the proceedings, and that the budget is being used to control the senators. These [statements] touched not just the merits of the case but also attack the integrity of the court,” Tolosa said in a press conference.

“We've always been asking for a fair shake. One court, one rule—let's apply them evenly. I am quite sure no one from the prosecution said anything that could be remotely considered to have attacked the integrity of the court and not even one senator-judge,” he added.
Tolosa said the statements from the Vice President's camp were intended to condition the minds of her supporters into believing that the proceedings were not legitimate.

“That’s why we will be asking the court to take action not just on the statements of the Vice President but also on the statements given by her spokesperson that have repeatedly violated the sub judice rule as well and which are even contemptuous in nature,” he added.
Tolosa also said he was prepared to respond to Sison's allegations.

“We look forward to receiving this motion that they may be filing, and we will respond to it accordingly. We've always respected the sub judice rule and the court's authority and integrity, as well as the integrity of the proceedings,” Tolosa said. —VBL, GMA News
