articles.title: Lions and tigers are kept legally in Ontario backyards. No one knows how many there are
articles.summary: Lions and tigers are among some of the most recognizable and dangerous predators in the world. They're also legal to own in Ontario, where provincial authorities can't say how many are being held in…

blocks.text: The secret tiger next door: inside Ontario's world of privately-owned big cats
People can legally keep lions or tigers in Ontario backyards, but provincial authorities don't know how many of the predators live in captivity across the province.
Ontario is the only province in Canada that has no licensing or permit system for keeping non-native wild animals, leaving it up to municipalities to decide what species residents can own.

In Wainfleet, Ont., a rural municipality 43 kilometres southwest of Niagara Falls, dangerous exotic animals became such a persistent problem that the township wrote its own rules in 2018 to give local authorities the tools to address the issue.

Enforcing it all falls to chief bylaw officer Mark Tardif, whose work has included policing a veritable Noah's Ark of exotic animals, from primates and sugar gliders (a type of exotic gliding possum), to pythons and tigers.
"A lot of tigers, probably five, six tigers, a jaguar, lemurs, kangaroos, water buffaloes," he said. "Snakes, unfortunately, lots of snakes."
Among his cases were dozens of animal escapes from a roadside zoo called Ringtail Ranch and, this spring, a Wainfleet resident who kept several tigers on a local property.

Zohaib Masood is shown with a juvenile tiger he kept on a property in Wainfleet along with two adult tigers and a hyena. The juvenile tiger and hyena were seized by Ontario's animal welfare services inspector. (Submitted by Zohaib Masood)
Whenever he deals with a call involving big cats, Tardif says he leaves himself an escape route.
"I usually leave my vehicle running and the door open, in case I have to bolt."
He says his protective vest was never designed for those kinds of encounters.
"I don't know how well this would hold up on a tiger bite," he said. "I want to go home at the end of the day. I have a family. So I do what I need to do."
Big cats, missing numbers

Wainfleet's bylaws require owners to register their exotic animals with provincial animal welfare authorities, but getting a clear picture of provincewide exotic animal ownership and related incidents from government records has proven difficult.
While Ontario allows people to keep dangerous predators, there is no provincewide system to account for them.

Two privately-owned tigers, seen here in an enclosure in Wainfleet, Ont. There are no federal or provincial rules when it comes to the ownership of dangerous exotic animals in Ontario, leaving monitoring and enforcement up to municipalities. (Mark Tardif/Township of Wainfleet)
Emergency responders might arrive at a property without knowing a lion or a tiger is present and when a municipality forces an owner out, they simply move their animals to another community.

CBC News asked Ontario for records of complaints and seizures invovling privately-owned big cats, as well as any statistical reports on those animals between January 2020 and May 2026. The Ministry of the Solicitor General said the records aren't kept in a single database and estimated the work would cost $1,050 — the equivalent of 35 hours of search time at Ontario's standard FOI rate.

"The records responsive to this request are not maintained as a single centralized dataset," the ministry said in a letter to CBC News, indicating the data was scattered across multiple systems, files and departments.
The Ministry of the Solicitor General said the OPP has "no classification system that captures occurrences involving 'exotic or dangerous animals.' "
A serval lies in the hay within its enclosure at Roaring Cat Retreat in Grand Bend, Ont., in this June 2019 Instagram photo. (Roaring Cat Retreat/Instagram)
An access-to-information request to the RCMP by CBC News about any information tracking big cats in private ownership also returned no records.
The only federal agency that tracks big cats is Environment Canada and Climate Change Canada.

It said in an email that two live tigers were imported into Ontario between 2022 and October 2026. Import applications must identify the animals' intended destination, but tracking ownership transfers, births and deaths is "typically the purview of provincial authorities," the department said.
'Giant gap' in rules

Once lions and tigers are in Canada, Kendra Coulter, a professor at Huron University College who heads the Animal Ethics and Sustainability Leadership program, says Ontario has no provincewide system to track who keeps them, where they end up or how many are born here.

"Falling through the cracks would imply that there was a floor in place, that there's some sort of structure or infrastructure around these animals and around the public," said Kendra Coulter, a professor of management and organizational studies at Western University's Huron University College, where she heads the Animal Ethics and Sustainability Leadership program.
"This is a giant gap that needs to be addressed," she said.
Kendra Coulter is a professor at Huron University College and co-ordinator of the school's Animal Ethics and Sustainability Leadership program. (Submitted by Kendra Coulter)
Coulter says because Ontario lacks any rules about exotic ownership, there are "covert networks" where people knowingly buy, sell and give away dangerous animals.

"We have no firm evidence, though we have reports" from law enforcement and people speaking off the record to researchers, she said. "Law enforcement has told me that some of this is happening online with commercial trading sites, but often in code."
CBC has not idependently established that animals are traded through coded listings.

Exotic animal owners are often reluctant to speak about it publicly. CBC News approached two private owners and Bervie Zoological Park, a roadside zoo near Kincardine, about 220 km west of Toronto — all recently had big cats seized by provincial authorities. None agreed to speak about the issue on the record.

When such animals are seized, they are often handed over to accredited zoos by the province. Many of those facilities were also reluctant to discuss the issue on the record. Some representatives contacted by CBC News said they feared confrontations with owners seeking to reclaim their animals.
Jungle Cat World Wildlife Park, a roadside zoo in Clarington, declined an interview and tour, but owner Peter Klose agreed to answer questions from CBC News by email.

"We believe that zoological facilities and research institutes with wildlife should be subject to provincial third-party oversight to ensure high animal welfare standards for all wildlife in captivity," he wrote when asked if Ontrario should introduce legislation governing the ownership of dangerous animals such as lions and tigers.
One town's ban, another town's problem
For Erin Ryan, the wildlife campaign manager at the animal welfare non-profit World Animal Protection, the bigger question is how those animals end up in private hands in the first place.

"Without any type of zoo licensing system or any type of permitting scheme, there's no requirement to show that you have the expertise, the facilities or the resources to keep either the animals or the public when safe when these animals are transferred to new places," she said.
Big cats peer through a fence at Roaring Cat Retreat in Grand Bend, Ont., in 2019. (Colin Butler/CBC)

In 2018, Ringtail Ranch's animals moved from Wainfleet, in the Niagara Region. In 2019, the owner resurfaced in Grand Bend in southwestern Ontario. After a battle with municipal officials there, the owner moved to Maynooth, in southeastern Ontario the following year.
In 2022, when four of the ranch's lions killed and ate a tiger, the owners were allowed to choose where the surviving animals would be relocated.

Brent Ross, a spokesperson for the Ministry of the Solicitor General, said the animals "were rehomed in appropriate settings to ensure their well-being. The location of the animals remains confidential for the same reason."

"They simply pack up shop and just move somewhere else where there isn't a bylaw," Ryan said. "Municipal rules can force an owner to move. They don't establish whether the next property is equipped to take the animals."
For Ryan, the question is what happens when the animals get to the next address.
"Municipal rules can force an owner to move. They don't establish whether the next property is equipped to take the animals," she said.

Coulter and her research assistants at Huron University College examined the bylaws of all 444 Ontario municipalities in 2020. At the time, half had no mention of ownership of non-native wild animals.
"You move 15 minutes west into the next county and there's no prohibitions," she said. "You can keep a tiger in your backyard."

In other words, municipalities can force dangerous animals out by creating bylaws, but without provincial laws governing where they're allowed, enforcing a bylaw in one town often shifts the responsibility to another place, resulting in a patchwork of rules.
Proposed rules, but no progress

There was an attempt to introduce a clear set of rules for Ontario in 2025 through Bill 35, a Liberal private member's bill that would require zoo licences, annual inspections and inventories recording births, deaths and transfers of non-native animals.

Under the proposed legislation, existing owners would be allowed to keep their animals, but would have to register them and undergo annual inspections. The legislation appears to have stalled. According to the Ontario legislature website, Bill 35 hasn't advanced beyond first reading since May 29, 2025.

CBC News reached out to Kanata-Carleton Liberal MPP Karen McCrimmon who sponsored the bill. Her office said it remains "in limbo" and they don't know if it will move forward in this legislative session.
Back in Wainfleet, Tardif stops short of saying whether the province needs clearer rules to govern the private ownership of exotic animals.

"I have no control over what the federal government does and provincial government does," he said. "It makes everyone's job hard, but these are the tools we have to work with and the legislation we have to work under."

articles.title: Why health care for Canadian women veterans is falling short
articles.summary: Women are the fastest growing segment of Canada’s veteran population, but they have complex physical and mental health problems that often get treated in isolation. A report released in June…

image.caption: A Canadian flag patch is shown on a soldier's shoulder in Trenton, Ont., in October 2014. A recent report calls for 'urgent, co-ordinated action' to address gaps in for female veterans. (Lars Hagberg/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: It started with the boots.

Wanda Motard is a size five-and-a-half in women's footwear. But when she was in basic training at Saint-Jean Garrison in Quebec in 2002, the only options were men's boots that didn't even begin to fit.
So despite the August heat, Motard says she would double up on thick wool socks and try to make do.

"I was constantly tripping over my feet, had rolled my ankle a few times, [which] led to a sprain," she told Dr. Brian Goldman, host of White Coat, Black Art. "With the forced marches, it became really, really difficult once I had my rucksack on."
The ill-fitting backpack left Mortard hunched over, compounding her struggles.
"But you know, the military is: one man, one kit."
Motard says she coped by getting off-the-shelf insoles, loading up on anti-inflammatory meds and icing her feet every night.
LISTEN | Motar's search for answers:
White Coat Black Art26:3020 years of pain: A woman veteran’s search for answers

Halfway through her basic training, Motard got boots that fit. But those early experiences were just the beginning of a series of problems that — more than two decades after she first joined Canada's Armed Forces (CAF) — have left the 47-year-old veteran with complex physical and emotional health problems, including chronic pain.

She's not alone. Roughly half of all veterans live with chronic pain, which for women veterans is more than double the number among Canada's general population, according to a joint report from the Chronic Pain Centre of Excellence for Canadian Veterans and the Canadian Pain Society.
The report, which came out in June, called for "urgent, co-ordinated action" to address gaps in care.

"We know that women veterans have different health outcomes from women civilians," said Alice Aiken, founder of the Canadian Institute for Military and Veteran Health, and professor of physiotherapy at Dalhousie University in Halifax.
While the report on chronic pain didn't explain the causes, said Aiken, it's important to monitor "because it can be a gateway for disability."
Nearly half of Women Veterans Council resigns in protest
Aiken, who has a PhD in health policy and is herself a veteran, said military jobs can be "very physically demanding" and come with more opportunities for injury and other sources of physical pain.
And she says many female members of the Forces have experiences similar to what Motard went through with ill-fitting equipment.

"A lot of the uniforms were not and are not designed specifically for women. They don't fit properly," said Aiken. "And so they're also then subject to potentially more injury and more reasons for chronic pain."
Not enough research

But there's a gap in research about women's experiences. Aiken says less than 10 per cent of publicly funded research dollars go to health research specific to women and research on women veterans is even more sparse.

When the House of Commons standing committee on veterans affairs released its 2024 report Invisible No More about the plight of women veterans, the first of its 41 recommendations was to launch a comprehensive research program, notes Aiken.

items: Women are a growing group of Canadian military veterans, but services are lagging
Veterans, families call for better access to make claims for exposure-related illness

blocks.text: Additionally, there can be a tough transition in terms of where veterans find care.
While they're in the Forces, people receive their health care from a separate military system, which Aiken describes as "probably one of the best health systems in Canada."
Soldiers board a CC-150 Polaris aircraft at CFB Greenwood in Nova Scotia in October 2014. (LS Eduardo Jorge/Combat Camera/Canadian Forces)
In that system there's a more interdisciplinary approach, in which any clinician can refer a patient to other health professions, says Aiken.
Once they leave the military, though, veterans are left navigating the health-care system in their province or territory.
Aiken praises publicly funded health care but says it "doesn't recognize, necessarily, the unique health needs of veterans and in particular women veterans."
Help from a private clinic
Into that gap has sprung at least one private clinic where a longtime military doctor, Dr. Markus Besemann, opened Beechwood Physical Medicine in Ottawa in 2022.
Besemann is a physiatrist, an expert in rehabilitation medicine. His 37-year career in the Forces included being chief of its rehabilitation program from 2008 to 2023.

When Besemann retired from the military, he and chiropractor Dr. Geoff Outerbridge founded Beechwood "to look after many people in pain but, amongst others, to focus on veterans and chronic pain," he said.
Dr. Markus Besemann, a longtime military doctor, opened Beechwood Physical Medicine in Ottawa in 2022, along with chiropractor Dr. Geoff Outerbridge. (Brian Goldman/CBC)

For some services the clinic offers, patients may be able to seek funding from Veterans Affairs Canada (VAC), but for others they'll need to pay out of pocket or seek reimbursement through any group health benefit programs they have access to.
Motard is one of their patients. She says she was put on a waitlist for a physiatrist in the public system after she left the military, but started searching online for other options during her wait.
Motard, who lives in the region of Gatineau, Que., across the river from Ottawa, says that search led her to Besemann, whose patient she'd been for five years when they were both in the military.
She says she was drawn to the integrated care Beechwood offered, where clinicians ranging from physicians to physiotherapists to psychologists and acupuncturists are together under one roof.
The mental health side of what they do is important, says Besemann.
"The simple sentence, I think, that says everything is, medicine is all about 'What's wrong with you? What's the diagnosis?' And trauma-informed care, I think, is 'What happened to you?'"
Sexual harassment a factor for many
Aiken said that while there isn't research on Canadian veterans specific to this topic, research on U.S. veterans suggests "military sexual trauma can also be a contributor to chronic pain."
To that end, Motard says the support she's had from Beechwood clinic includes seeing psychotherapist Mary Marcolin to address problems that include sexual harassment.

While in the Forces, Motard says the harassment she experienced "ranged anywhere from inappropriate comments, unwelcome comments, to inappropriate touching, pressure to enter into sexual relationships, right up to threats and stalking, essentially," Motard said.

She was a member of a class-action lawsuit against the Department of National Defence (DND) for sexual misconduct, which was settled in 2019, with the federal government agreeing to compensate those affected and take steps to make the military a safer and more respectful workplace.
In 2021, the Forces, the federal government and the DND issued a public apology.
A 2025 report found the military made significant progress in changing the culture around sexual misconduct, though it said more work is needed to make those changes last.

items: Women in Canadian military subjected to harassment, discrimination, suit alleges
Head of Veterans Affairs office that supports women disappointed by misconduct allegations against top brass

blocks.text: DND said in an email to CBC News that it is "addressing sexual misconduct through a sustained culture change effort."
It also said, among other things, that "a contoured combat uniform designed around female morphology" will begin to go into service in 2027, with similarly updated body armour to follow in 2028.
A spokesperson for Veterans Affairs says the department recognizes the complex needs of veterans living with chronic pain, and offers coverage for a range of physical and mental health services.
The spokesperson also said VAC is working to address gaps in care and in research on the health of women veterans.

articles.title: Chinese authorities blocked Canada's Tiananmen Square tribute with trees, cherry picker: documents
articles.summary: Chinese authorities blocked attempts by the Canadian embassy to visually commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre for the last two years, CBC News has learned.

image.caption: Two trees block an LED display in front of the Canadian Embassy in Beijing, in a photo CBC News obtained through an access to information request. An embassy staffer writes the trees were planted by local authorities days before Canada intended to display the image of a candle to commemorate the Tia

blocks.text: Politics·New
Chinese authorities blocked attempts by the Canadian embassy to visually commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre for the last two years, CBC News has learned.
Global Affairs also shortened draft social media post on massacre prior to publication
Chinese authorities blocked attempts by the Canadian Embassy to visually commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre for the last two years, CBC News has learned.
The second incident came just months after Prime Minister Mark Carney's trade trip to Beijing, where he touted improved relations with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

"Late Saturday evening local authorities, working into the early hours of Sunday, planted two large, mature trees in an attempt to block the embassy's LED screen," noted an email by Diana Tan, a staffer at the Canadian Embassy in Beijing, obtained by CBC News through an access to information request.
The message was dated June 1, three days before the Canadian diplomatic mission intended to display an image of a candle to mark the Tiananmen Square massacre's 37th anniversary.
"The trees were planted on municipal property, approximately 0.5-1 metre from the embassy wall," Tan noted.

Another document released as part of the access to information package notes that in 2025, "the Chinese government sent a crane to suspend a large rectangular barrier in front of the screen of the embassy so that passersby could not see the candle."
A boom lift partially blocks the view of a screen depicting a lit candle at the Canadian Embassy on the Tiananmen Square massacre anniversary last year. (Ng Han Guan/The Associated Press)

China remains sensitive to remarks about the Tiananmen Square massacre, when tanks and soldiers cracked down on unarmed protesters seeking political reform, transparency and freedom of the press. Background information in the documents note the death toll estimates range from several hundred to several thousand.

The documents obtained by CBC News, largely redacted, suggest 2024 was the first time the Canadian Embassy in Beijing displayed the image of the candle on its LED screen. Though the unredacted portions make no mention of the image getting blocked that year, they do state the projection "led to security officials contacting the embassy."

"The projector image of a candle in Beijing is an important tool for public communications used for the last two years to ensure some level of local visibility since social media posts in China will likely face some kind of censorship," the documents note.
Revisions for 'commemorative tone'
The documents also reveal Global Affairs initially intended to publish a two-paragraph statement on the social media platform X this year to commemorate the event.

In an email sent June 1, hours after the one from embassy staff sharing the news of the planted trees, senior communications adviser Meghan O'Brien sought clearance for the post's publication. The first paragraph of the draft post is redacted.

The response from Mike Williams, who is identified in the emails as deputy director for the Greater China Political and Coordination Division, reads: "Modified single tweet, rather than 2 short tweets. Also revised message to commemorative tone focused on victims/families."

The post Global Affairs wound up publishing in full on X reads: "Today, Canadians honour the memory of all who lost their lives, were injured or went missing during the Tiananmen Square crackdown on June 4, 1989. Canada stands with the survivors and the families and loved ones who continue to demand accountability."

That post raised eyebrows online, many noting the use of the word crackdown instead of massacre. Former Alberta premier and federal Conservative defence minister Jason Kenney called it a "deliberate misuse of language to minimize the massacre."
Conservative MP Andrew Lawton wrote "stop letting [Liberal MP] Michael Ma write your tweets."

items: Canada faces fresh scrutiny, calls to do more to prevent Canadian corporate abuses abroad

blocks.text: Statements on X, one of many U.S. social media platforms blocked in China, have gone further in previous years.
In 2025, the department named China, calling on the country "to uphold its human rights obligations under international law."

In 2024, Mélanie Joly, then minister of foreign affairs, wrote: "Canada calls on China to uphold its human rights obligations under international law and we will continue to speak for those who cannot speak freely and stand with those who stand for human dignity."

The documents also note that China did not censor a Canadian Embassy post on Chinese social media platform Weibo in 2025, saying it was the first time Beijing did not do so. Redacted portions of the documents show Canadian officials prepared alternative statements to be posted on Weibo in case the initial one was taken down this year.
The Canadian government has never publicly spoken about either attempts at blocking the LED screen, nor provided an explanation about the wording of the social media post published on X this year.
CBC News has reached out to Global Affairs, the Prime Minister's Office and the Chinese Embassy in Canada for comment.
Prime Minister Mark Carney met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing at the start of the year. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)
Carney is expected to return to China this month to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

He has met with Chinese President Xi Jinping twice so far in his capacity as prime minister. The two first attempted to reset relations during a one-on-one in South Korea in November 2025, on the margins of last year's APEC summit, before Carney's visit to Beijing in January.
Ties between Canada and China were fraught under Carney's predecessor Justin Trudeau, with Canada arresting Chinese tech executive Meng Wanzhou in December 2018 as she faced fraud charges in the U.S.
Days later, the Chinese government imprisoned Canadians Michael Spavor and Michael Kovrig for alleged espionage — eventually releasing them in 2021.
The public inquiry into foreign election interference also found China to be one of the chief state actors attempting to intervene in Canadian elections in 2019 and 2021.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Raffy Boudjikanian is a senior reporter with the CBC's Parliamentary Bureau in Ottawa. He has also worked in Edmonton, Calgary and Montreal for the public broadcaster.

articles.title: COP31: What the Philippines wants for the ocean
articles.summary: Among the Philippine delegation's calls at COP31 is 'stopping further offshore fossil fuel expansion'

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The Philippine delegation at the United Nations (UN) Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, brings an ocean agenda consistent with the demands of neighboring Pacific island nations and civil society.

Environment Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna, who heads the Philippine delegation in Turkey, said they expect this year’s conference to become “a true COP of implementation focused on actual results rather than unfulfilled roadmaps.”
“The Philippines calls for urgent climate finance disbursements for adaptation alongside rapid response policies for loss and damage,” Cuna said in a message sent to Rappler on Monday, November 9.

The delegation considers these agenda items as “nonnegotiable priorities”: the adoption of the Antalya Ocean Declaration, the creation of permanent ocean-related agenda items across the UN climate process, stronger commitments from rich nations, and dedicated financing for ocean and coastal communities.
These are strong calls, consistent with the Pacific region. These are countries facing the same climate threats of rising sea levels and the devastating impact of ocean warming on marine life.

The Philippines “urged developed countries to take the lead in ocean-based mitigation by establishing binding offshore wind targets, launching green maritime corridors, and stopping further offshore fossil fuel expansion,” said the Department of Environment and Natural Resources’ statement sent to Rappler.
Moreover, the Philippines “stressed the need” to create “ocean funding windows under the Green Climate Fund, GEF-9, and the loss and damage fund.”

The Philippines, home to the richest marine biodiversity in the world, needs to be at the forefront of prioritizing ocean solutions in its national climate plan, said Martha Vergara, deputy head for oceans and climate at the Center for Energy, Ecology, and Development (CEED).
One of CEED’s campaigns is its opposition to liquefied natural gas facilities that crowd in the Verde Island Passage.

“Gas infrastructure and oil and gas exploration are being pushed into the very waters that feed our communities, while a very strong El Niño is projected to strain water and food supplies,” Vergara said in a statement Tuesday, November 10.

blocks.caption: OPENING. André Corrêa do Lago, COP30 president, makes a statement during the opening of COP31 in Turkey on November 9, 2026. Photo by Kiara Worth/UNClimateChange

blocks.text: A resounding call at this climate summit is the need to translate declarations and commitments into actions felt on the ground.
This is not new. In fact, the climate summit held in Brazil in 2025 was billed as “Implementation COP.”

“For COP31 to truly be a Blue COP, global leaders must not stop at honoring the ocean in pledges and declarations,” said Vergara. “They need to deliver the resources to realize the protection of our seas in a high-integrity manner.”
On the first day of COP31, Pacific envoys underlined the ocean agenda and their desire for this summit to be remembered as the “Blue COP.”

Three Pacific COP31 envoys were appointed to reflect the ocean and climate priorities of the Pacific island nations: Tina Stege from the Marshall Islands, Ruel Yamuna from Papua New Guinea, and Inia Seruiratu from Fiji.
Stege urged world leaders to show “political will and urgency” to keep 1.5 degrees Celsius within reach.

“It means delivering predictable and accessible climate finance while increasing investment in ocean and forest stewardship, climate resilience, and sustainable blue economies,” Stege said in a press conference on Monday.
“The Pacific helped secure the inclusion of 1.5 degrees Celsius under the Paris Agreement,” she added. “And 10 years later, we remain steadfast in our commitment to that goal.” – Rappler.com

This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership, a journalism fellowship organized by Internews’ Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth, and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

articles.title: Why electrification is the climate game changer we need
articles.summary: From EVs and electric buses on the road, heat pumps warming homes and solar panels powering appliances, the shift to electrifying tech is already in full swing. But what exactly does…

image.caption: Replacing fossil fuels with clean electricity is key to cutting emissionsImage: Barbara Gindl/APA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Electrification isn't just a buzzword, it's a lever that could slash energy bills while reducing the world's dependency on coal, oil and gas. Which also means significantly slashing the heat-trapping CO2 emissions that are linked to flooding and extreme heat around the world.

If fuel-importing countries "speed up the electrification of their economies considerably" they could knock more than $400 billion (€357 billion) off their energy import bills by 2035 compared with 2025 levels.
That is according to a recent analysis by the
which also found that such an acceleration could mean the world needs 18 million fewer barrels of oil per day.
What exactly is electrification?

In a nutshell, electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels such as oil and gas with electric alternatives. That means switching from diesel cars to electric vehicles (EVs), turning off gas heating and using electricity to power heat pumps.

But the way the electricity running these things is generated is also important. In theory, an EV using power created in a coal-heavy electricity grid could be worse for the climate than a car running on gas.
Electricity derived from renewable energy sources such as solar, wind or hydropower on the other hand produces clean power.
How countries are skipping 200 years of carbon emissions
Where are we right now with global electrification?
The booming EV market is the fastest-growing electrification sector. Globally, one in four cars sold in 2025 was electric and since 2020, international sales have increased by almost 600%.
Nonetheless, electricity only covers about 20% of final energy use in the wider global economy, including that used in businesses, factories and people's homes.
It would need to supply more than half of all power by 2050 if we are to avoid runaway heating and the more intense and extreme weather events connected to a hotter climate.
Are there any limitations to what we can electrify?

Some industries and activities are harder to electrify than others. While it's relatively easy to switch to EVs and decarbonize buildings, some industries such as petrochemicals and steel use fossil fuels as raw materials to make products like plastics, fertilizer, detergent or steel.
In addition, while heat pumps work well for low-temperature needs, they can't replace the temperatures needed in steelmaking or cement production.

Independent research organization the World Resources Institute recommends hydrogen, synthetic fuels or other low-carbon alternatives as more viable options than electrification in cases such as ocean shipping and aviation.
Can aviation become more sustainable?
What are the benefits of electrification?
In addition to cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions resulting in cleaner air and limiting global heating, electrification is also more efficient and cheaper in the long run.

A combustion engine in a car wastes as much as 80% of its fuel's energy, mostly to turn it into heat. Only about 20% is converted to actually move the car. Electric motors, on the other hand, convert about 80% of electrical energy into motion.

As the World Resources Institute points out, running all appliances on electricity will increase electricity consumption. Yet total energy costs are likely to be lower, even if electricity becomes more expensive.
Any challenges to electrification?

As electricity needs grow due to the rapid expansion of AI, data centers and the overall shift to a more electrified world, outpaced grids struggle to keep up. This is increasingly holding back the energy transition, delaying the rollout of additional renewable generation, storage capacity, and electrified demand.
According to the IEA, annual grid investment has to increase about 50% by 2030 from today's $400 billion.

There's also a major mismatch between how long it takes to set up new grid infrastructure (5 to 15 years), compared to renewable energy projects (1 to 5 years), and EV charging infrastructure (1 to 2 years).
Experts say we need smarter grids that support a two-way flow of electricity while remaining secure, stable and able to keep up with higher demand as electrification intensifies.

articles.title: Cop31 live: slight drop in fossil fuel emissions revealed as conference enters second day
articles.summary:
UN climate summit prepares to host world leaders from more than 90 countries tomorrow

In an attempt to get to the venue a bit early, I decided to ditch the tram and try the special Cop31…

blocks.text: Opening summary: world's fever rapidly worsening as conference enters day 2

blocks.caption: Oliver Milman

blocks.text: Oliver Milman
Good morning from Turkey and welcome to the second day of Cop31, the UN gathering that is taking place, again, to help prod indolent countries clear of catastrophic planetary heating.

A lot of angst was vented on the first day of the summit over whether this goal is being achieved, and even if Cop is the best forum in which to achieve it. Perhaps sensing the fractured, distracted geopolitical mood, Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate minister and Cop negotiations chief, plaintively urged countries to “show the world that multilateralism works. Let’s show the world we are equal to the challenge.”

Further evidence, if it was needed, was unveiled yesterday showing the world is failing rather badly in this challenge to stem its growing fever. But research published this morning shows carbon emissions from fossil fuels are falling slightly, and there is still hope here in Antalya that things can change. If not then, well, what are we all doing here? Right?

About 100,000 delegates crammed into the well-tended conference venue yesterday and the long queues for registration badges led the UN to plead for people to return for them today if attendance on Monday wasn’t compulsory.

Tuesday will lay the groundwork for the arrival tomorrow of leaders from more than 90 countries, with notable absentees including the heads of the US and China. Today’s theme is “energy and transport, touching on a key goal of this Cop to get the world to agree to greatly increase the share of energy used via electricity”. That power will, hopefully, be clean.

Let’s see how close to consensus the world will be on that. At the very least, the Turkish baked goods promise to be delicious and there is some tasteful art constructed of discarded waste to look at. Onwards.

blocks.text: Carbon pollution flatlined in 2026, scientists find

blocks.caption: Fiona Harvey

blocks.text: Fiona Harvey
Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.

Carbon dioxide from oil, gas and coal is forecast to flatline for 2026, based on data from the year so far, according to a comprehensive assessment by scientists. Emissions from burning oil alone will drop by 2% as drivers economise on fuel use and flock to electric vehicles instead.

The findings, presented on Tuesday morning at the Cop31 climate talks hosted by Turkey in Antalya, show both the impact of the Iran war and the global expansion of cheap renewable energy, chiefly solar and wind power.

Talk of a global turnaround would be premature, however, the report’s authors and other analysts said. The reduction in emissions from fossil fuels for 2026 will be about 0.4% compared with last year.

blocks.caption: A barge moving past a coal-fired power plant near New Haven, West Virginia, US. Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/AP

blocks.text: Yet this year’s slight fall could be temporary, and was more than offset by increased emissions from deforestation and land use change, following major fires in south-east Asia and further conversions of wild land to agriculture.

Many factors could disrupt the fragile trend of slowing emissions from fossil fuels, including an intensified expansion of coal in India, an easing of oil prices and US president Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for fossil fuels. Much greater investment in renewable energy, and low-carbon technology such as electric vehicles, would still be required to make permanent reductions in annual emissions, the report’s authors said.

blocks.caption: Graham Readfearn

blocks.text: Graham Readfearn
In an attempt to get to the venue a bit early, I decided to ditch the tram and try the special Cop31 buses. This was a bad decision.
We have just reached the two-and-a-half-hour mark on the bus and are still crawling through Antalya traffic. New friendships are being spawned in here. We are starting to eat each other’s food.
I want to thank Philippa Bayley from Groundwork for the walnut and chocolate biscuits she snaffled from her hotel buffet.
Exceptional, which is more than I can say for the traffic.

articles.title: DR Congo sentences 66 soldiers to death for being 'cowards'
articles.summary: The Congolese army's fight against rebel groups has long been hampered by disarray within its ranks.

blocks.text: At least 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in the Democratic Republic of Congo for cowardice, mutiny and refusing to obey orders, local media report.

The sentences followed a trial of 71 soldiers before a military court in Walikale, in North Kivu province, in eastern DR Congo. Four soldiers were acquitted, while another was sentenced to 10 years in prison.
The army said the trial was intended to improve discipline among troops as they battle armed groups in eastern DR Congo.
The region has endured decades of conflict, with fighting continuing between government forces and the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), a rebel coalition that includes the M23 group.
The soldiers were reportedly arrested on 20 October in Walikale, where they were accused of abandoning their positions and fleeing during clashes with FRN fighters.
The Congolese army's campaign against armed groups, including the M23, has long been undermined by poor discipline and disorganisation within its ranks.
The government has repeatedly accused neighbouring Rwanda of supporting the M23, an allegation denied by both Kigali and the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.
The army has faced persistent criticism over its lack of professionalism and disciplined, while soldiers have complained of poor pay and inadequate equipment.
Last month, another 27 soldiers were sentenced to death on similar charges of cowardice after reportedly withdrawing from the frontline during clashes with rebels.
In March 2024, DR Congo lifted a 20-year moratorium on the death penalty, citing the need to remove "traitors" within the army.
The government said capital punishment would also apply to people involved in armed groups, insurrection, as well as committing treason and war crimes.
The decision to reinstate the death penalty was widely criticised by rights groups. However, no formal executions have been carried out since the moratorium was lifted.
Since the beginning of 2025, at least 507 soldiers have been convicted, including 381 death sentences, according to figures compiled by French broadcaster RFI.

In October 2025, former Congolese President Joseph Kabila was sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself. He has since been named as the FRN's leader.

articles.title: Will Australia push for fossil fuel exit at UN talks?
articles.summary: The heat is on Australia as chief negotiator at the COP31 UN climate conference to forge a path away from coal and gas, and to protect Pacific neighbors facing rising sea levels.

image.caption: Australia will lead talks to address the climate crisis, yet remains the world's second-largest exporter of carbon-heavy coalImage: DW

blocks.text: In its role as president of negotiations at the upcoming UN climate talks in Turkey, Australia is being pressured to guide nations towards unified action on slashing the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions that are generated in large part by burning fossil fuels.
The nation has pledged to lead by example at the summit through a strong commitment to renewable energy, electrification and reduced reliance on planet-heating coal, oil and gas.

"Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," said Australian climate minister Chris Bowen in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.
"These are proven, commercial and scalable today. Now is the moment for faster implementation."

Yet Australia is also the world's third-largest exporter of fossil fuels. And unlike France and Germany, or island nations from Fiji to the Bahamas that are highly vulnerable to a changing climate, the COP31 co-president has not yet commited to phasing them out.
As calls grow for the country to set a clear route to a clean energy future, critics say its vague promise to transition away from polluting sources of power does not go far enough.

blocks.caption: Australia is planning for 82% renewable electricity in its grid by 2030. But fossil fuel projects continue to be approvedImage: ACT Government

blocks.text: Transition is also about energy security
Australia is home to 56% of global coal mine projects currently in the pipeline, notes environmental non-profit, 350.org.

Andreas Sieber, head of political strategy at the organization, is calling on the country, the world's second-largest coal exporter, to reverse course and announce an "overdue coal phaseout date" during the COP31 conference.
"Australia needs to walk the walk and follow Germany's example and commit to a phaseout," said Melanie Pill, founder of the Climate Project, an Australia-based climate policy advisory.
The argument to end fossil fuel production is not only about cutting emissions but reducing dependence on energy systems that rely on volatile oil and gas markets, she explained.
"A fossil phaseout in the face of the enduring and escalating conflict in the Middle East is in the interest of everyone," Pill told DW.
How Iran war energy crisis strengthens case for renewables

This is especially true for Australia's diesel-reliant Pacific neighbours, who spend up to 25% of GDP on fossil fuel imports — as opposed 6% on health — according to a report by the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of New South Wales.
As lead negotiator at the UN climate talks, Australia can "flip the narrative" on a fossil fuel phaseout, using the challenge of energy security as a justification, said Pill
Climate tsar still pushing coal and gas
This opportunity could be lost, however, if Australia fails to address fossil fuel exports that accounted for 80% of its total carbon footprint in 2022 — and near 5% of global emissions.

While the nation is a world leader in rooftop solar, and generates around half of its electricity from renewables, this progress is "being undone by its continued approval of more fossil fuels for export," said Simon Bradshaw, COP31 lead and climate expert at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

He notes that the Labor government of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has approved the construction, expansion or extension of 38 coal, oil and gas projects since coming to power four years ago on a pro-climate platform.

"You cannot aspire to lead on climate abroad if you're not getting your own house in order," said Thomas Houlie, climate and energy policy analyst at Climate Analytics, a global climate policy institute.

Last year, when Australia approved the extension of a major gas export project in the country's west until 2070, Albanese justified the move in the name of a balance between "security of energy supply" and "support [for] the transition which reduces our emissions."

blocks.caption: Australian coal arriving in China contributes to the 5% of global emissions derived from Australian fossil fuel exportsImage: Chen Weifeng/ChinaFotoPress/MaxpppP/picture-alliance

blocks.text: The country has publicly backed a global transition away from the fossil fuels driving the global temperature rise linked to extreme heat and drought. Both through the Global Stocktake agreed at the 2023 UN climate summit, and via the inaugural "transitioning away" summit in Colombia this April, at which Australia and 56 countries pledged to develop a fossil fuel exit roadmap.
But these commitments are not reflected in Australian resources policy, or its domestic rollout of clean power infrastructure.

"While the government has set a renewables target for electricity, it leaves plenty of blind spots in other sectors," said Houlie, adding that emission reductions in industry and transport have been limited and that the push to achieve an 82% renewables target for the electricity grid by 2030 is behind schedule.
Australia needs to step up for Pacific neighbors

In its role as lead negotiator at COP31, Australia has promised to ensure that any final conference text serves to "elevate the views and the experiences" of small Pacific nations in its region from Vanuatu to Tuvalu.

These island countries that generate low emissions yet suffer extreme climate impacts from worsening cyclones or rising seas are "sick of Australia's double talk on climate," said Shiva Gounden, Head of Pacific at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

Australia must commit to "substantial new funding contributions" to help Pacific neighbors adapt to the climate emergency and achieve energy independence, said Simon Bradshaw. He reiterated the need to concurrently create a "national road map" away from coal and gas production and export.

A Climate Analytics report co-authored by Houlie outlines a fossil fuel phaseout pathway for Australia that can begin immediately. This includes an end to coal power generation by 2034 and a rapid reduction in oil and gas consumption with renewables generating almost all the country's electricity by 2040. Fossil fuel export projects would be eliminated, and existing ones shuttered before becoming obsolete.
"This co-presidency is a golden opportunity for Australia to step up and commit to a phaseout," said Houlie.
Tuvalu – living with the reality of climate change

articles.title: Grenades, grief and a deepening political divide: five takeaways from Sonia Gandhi’s new memoir
articles.summary:
From the assassinations of her husband and mother-in-law to press stonewalling under Modi, Belonging offers an insider’s account of India’s political evolution

Few love stories have been as…

blocks.text: Few love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.

The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.)

Belonging, published today, contains moving glimpses of Gandhi’s private grief. She writes about the loss of her first child, who died shortly after birth, and the chilling discovery of grenades in a room of their house after Operation Blue Star, the 1984 military operation against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple in Amritsar. She also provides a ringside view of several turbulent chapters in Indian politics, not least the violent assassinations of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, in 1984 and her husband, Rajiv, in 1991.

Her book also revisits some of the darker episodes that have dogged the Gandhi family and the Congress party, including Indira’s imposition of the Emergency in June 1975, a 21-month period during which civil liberties were suspended, political opponents were jailed and the press was gagged, which caused fear and dismay across the country. In Gandhi’s account, italso caused a rift within the family.

Ultimately, Gandhi’s memoir is a vivid record of six decades of India’s political transformation from the Congress-dominated secular republic she moved to in 1968 until today, when Hindu nationalism has become the dominant political force under Narendra Modi.
Here are five key takeaways from her memoir and what they reveal about the state of Indian politics today.
Gandhi has had no real contact with Modi for the last 12 years

blocks.caption: Sonia Gandhi, widow of former Indian prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, shown in March 1998 when she was elected president of Congress party. Photograph: John Mcconnico/AP

blocks.text: Gandhi’s account offers a glimpse of how deep the political polarisation runs in Indian politics today. In one revealing passage, Gandhi writes that she has had “practically no real contact” with Modi in the 12 years he has led the nation. In fact, at times when the two have been in the same rooms, such as the speaker’s small chamber, Modi “tends to look away, avoiding eye contact”, she says. On occasion, she adds, he has asked briefly about her health after a hospital stay.

For her, this breakdown is a departure from the past, when leaders on opposing sides of the aisle “would treat one another with cordiality”. After the 2001 terror attack on parliament, Gandhi immediately called then-BJP prime minister AB Vajpayee to enquire about his safety, a gesture he appreciated.

Gandhi sees an increasingly authoritarian style of politics, in which those in power seek to “belittle and torment” opponents. For years, Gandhi’s son, Rahul, has been the subject of BJP’s ridicule, which calls him Pappu, a derisive term intended to portray him as inexperienced and naive. She adds that similar things are happening elsewhere in the world, an observation that can be read in the context of US President Donald Trump’s use of personal insults and ridicule against opponents.
It’s lonely at the top for India’s female politicians

India has an illustrious history of women occupying top leadership positions, long before many other democracies. But their rise has often come at a cost – that of loneliness in navigating a male-dominated political world.

In the book, Gandhi describes a 2012 conversation with Hillary Clinton on the countrys’ female leaders and their backgrounds. In her recollections of Indira, she shares that, despite wielding authority, Indira could feel besieged and profoundly alone, and this was particularly acute, Gandhi writes, in the months leading up to the declaration of the Emergency by her mother-in-law.
Gandhi also writes of her own isolation, including when she decided to take on the leadership of the Congress out of a sense of duty to her family’s political legacy.
Those in power are increasingly stonewalling the press

blocks.caption: A poster showing Indian prime minister Narendra Modi at a protest by the Congress party and its allies in New Delhi on 1 November. Photograph: Manish Swarup/AP

blocks.text: Among the many ways in which Gandhi charts the erosion of India’s democratic conventions in Belonging, one particularly telling shift is the changed relationship between the media and those in power. She recalls a time when journalists had opportunities to question prime ministers directly.

In 12 years in power, Modi has not addressed a single press conference on his own. He has sat in on one press briefing at the conclusion of an election campaign, and appeared alongside US presidents at joint press encounters after bilateral meetings, where they took questions from the press. Modi has consistently avoided facing journalists in an open forum, and his media interactions have largely been one-on-one interviews with sympathetic, pro-government news anchors or in one much publicised exchange with a Bollywood actor who asked him how he liked to eat mangoes.
And it’s not just media …

The book’s publication has brought renewed attention to concerns about the space for free expression in contemporary India, and the extent to which apprehensions about repercussions may influence what can be said, written and published.

Penguin Random House India was to publish Gandhi’s memoir but withdrew from the project in August. Gandhi told the Guardian that it was “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and said it had dropped the book after she declined certain suggested edits. Penguin has disputed her account, saying that the suggestion it decided not to publish the book because of refused editorial changes “does not accurately reflect the circumstances”.
The book, released in the US by Alfred A Knopf, is being published in India by HarperCollins.

In June, Penguin had also pulled out of plans to distribute graphic journalist Joe Sacco’s The Once and Future Riot, about the 2013 Muzaffarnagar communal violence. The publisher cited an inaccurate map of India and unresolved citation issues. Sacco, however, blamed the decision on the “current political climate in India”.
She’s had quiet fallouts with the ‘thoroughly dishonest’

Western political memoirs, particularly by former heads of government or senior politicians, are often forthcoming in naming political adversaries, recounting private exchanges and offering candid assessments of colleagues. David Cameron’s 2019 memoir, For the Record, took aim at his former friend, Michael Gove, describing him as “mendacious” and a “foam-flecked Faragist”.
after newsletter promotion

Gandhi, in contrast, is restrained. She writes warmly of the closeness between the Gandhi family and that of Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan, whose parents she lived with when she first moved to India, but she makes no mention of the subsequent estrangement between the two families. In another instance, she does not name the political leader she describes as “thoroughly dishonest” and who she says she trusted in 1999, when Congress unsuccessfully attempted to form a coalition government.
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: A painting from the series, When No One Moves by Baaraan Ijlal, who is showing at Art Mumbai. Photograph: Artist Baaraan Ijlal

blocks.text: Art | Art Mumbai runs from 12-15 November at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse. Among the highlights of this year’s edition is artist Baaraan Ijlal’s collaboration with the celebrated lyricist Javed Akhtar, turning his evocative Urdu couplets into paintings. The two will be in conversation with curator Ranjit Hoskote on Friday.

Government | The official bungalow of Andhra Pradesh’s chief minister, N Chandrababu Naidu, was renovated by a government-owned enterprise for Rs 6.5 crore (£518,000), according to the Indian Express (£). The renovation work on the Delhi property included was said to have had a major makeover.

Film | Bollywood’s ambitious rendering of Hindu epic Ramayana, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Sai Pallavi, was released on 5 November. Touted as the most expensive Indian film ever made, it earned praise from the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw, who described it as “thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular”.
Your Diwali celebrations
Readers from India and around the world on the festival of lights and tell us how they celebrated.

blocks.caption: Diwali celebrations have touched readers around the world. Photograph: Firdous Nazir/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: double quotation markIn India, Diwali comes to you. You can see it in the streets, hear it in the neighbourhood and feel it in the atmosphere. In the UK, it is different. Life carries on around you. But traditions do not have to disappear when you move countries – they can change shape. A small light in a quiet room can carry the same meaning as an entire street illuminated for Diwali. Aman, Plymouth, UK

double quotation markMy favorite part of Diwali back home was getting up before sunrise on Narak Chaturdashi and having a ceremonial bath, followed by a breakfast of traditional Marathi Diwali snacks. I have been living abroad for over 10 years now and it’s always a bittersweet time of the year where I miss my family and the general vibe of Diwali in India. But I am trying to build new traditions as one half of an Indian-Austrian couple, which includes trading the traditional boxes of mithai for Manner Schnitten and marzipan. Charu, Germany

double quotation markThere used to be more of a community spirit to Diwali. As kids, we would be tasked with going door to door, exchanging sweets and snacks with neighbours (sometimes to our great displeasure, because it made for awkward conversation with those we had annoyed with our antics). Nowadays, the celebrations are mostly private. Group celebrations are walled off within exclusive clubs, families light their own fireworks almost competitively, and people send each other sweets through a delivery service. Samyuktha, Chennai
Count it
A number worth knowing
The government has approved the sale of a 60.7% stake in IDBI bank to Canadian Fairfax Holdings for Rs 52,878 crore (£4.22bn).
Vibe check

blocks.caption: Now you see it … freestyler Riswan’s football tricks have gone viral on Instagram. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: It’s hard to take one’s eyes off Muhammed Riswan when he’s at work. The 23-year-old football freestyler from Areekode in Kerala’s Malappuram district conjures tricks with the ball in a delicately choreographed dance. It glides between his feet, next it is rolling on to his back right before he leaps into the air to catch it with one hand.
Riswan, who’s been freestyling for eight years, is one of the two Indians to win Instagram Rings 2026 award recognising creators. The other is Chanel model Bhavitha Mandava.

Riswan’s big break came with a video filmed at Keralamkundu waterfall, where he pulled off a freestyle move before gracefully arching the ball into the water. The clip has since clocked more than 600m views. Last year, he was invited to watch his sporting idol, Lionel Messi, play in Argentina.
Get in touch

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.
