blocks.text: November 10, 2026
Ukraine's Zelenskyy in Denmark for talks with Nordic leaders

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has arrived in Denmark, where he is to hold meetings with Nordic leaders on military support, air defense and energy infrastructure security amid Russia's invasion of his country, Danish authorities said.

"I am proud to welcome President Zelenskyy and the Nordic leaders to Denmark. The Ukrainians' fight for a free Ukraine and a free Europe continues," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said in a statement.
"Almost five years after the full-scale invasion, the rain of bombs targeting civilians, relief centers, and water and heating plants continues. That is why we must stand firm," Frederiksen said.
Zelenskyy's trip comes as the US-mediated talks on the conflict in Ukraine between Kyiv and Moscow kick off in Abu Dhabi.

articles.title: Author Jojo Moyes among UK travellers at risk of EU ban amid digital border system glitches
articles.summary: Errors in entry and exit records leave some Britons wrongly flagged as having overstayed post-Brexit 90-day limit

blocks.text: The writer Jojo Moyes is facing a two-year EU travel ban and €10,000 (£8,300) fine because of glitches with the bloc’s digital security controls.
She is one of a number of UK travellers who say their trips to the EU have not been properly recorded since the introduction of the EU digital entry and exit system (EES).
The system, which launched last year, has replaced passport stamps with biometrics recorded at border control in Schengen zone countries.
However, the botched rollout has led to some Britons being denied their post-Brexit right to spend 90 days out of 180 in Europe because the system falsely states they have used up their allowance.
Moyes, a bestselling novelist, was detained by French border guards after a holiday and accused of overstaying. She had spent only 23 days in the EU over six months.
She discovered that her departure from Portugal after a trip in May had not been logged on the system.

“The clock had been ticking ever since,” she told the consumer organisation Which? “The border control senior officer at Marseille warned me that I should not attempt to re-enter Europe until it is sorted out, or face a €10,000 fine and a two-year ban.”

blocks.caption: Jojo Moyes was detained by French border guards after a holiday and accused of overstaying. Photograph: Which

blocks.text: Over the summer, some countries suspended the EES and resorted to manual passport checks due to technical glitches and staff shortages. On Monday, it emerged that the EU is suing three firms over the failures.
The problem affects passengers whose biometrics were collected on their arrival in the EU, but not on their departure. In some cases, this means the system has failed to record that they have left.
The rolling 180-day window starts as soon as they enter the EU and, since Brexit, those who are deemed to have remained for more than 90 days face deportation or fines of up to €10,000.

Jane Nolan and her husband discovered that the EES wrongly showed them as having used up their 90-day travel allowance, preventing them from booking a trip to France. “We travelled to France in April by LeShuttle and spent 40 days there,” she said. “We have made no subsequent Schengen visits.

“We should have 50 days remaining, but the EU’s ‘check how long you can stay’ tool says: ‘Authorised stay: not OK,’ and zero remaining days. It does not show us which entry or exit record produced that result.”
The couple’s passports were manually stamped on their return to the UK in June as French authorities had suspended the EES to prevent long queues.
“We have asked the French authorities to check our records, but do not yet know what has gone wrong or whether the result could affect us at the border,” said Nolan.
In a case reported by the Telegraph a holidaymaker from the UK was detained at the Italian border and deported under police guard after a system error suggested she had overstayed in the EU.
Rory Boland, Editor of Which? Travel described the situation as unacceptable.

“This is one of the most serious in a long line of European border control failures,” he said. “The lack of care and accountability shown towards travellers, who risk being locked up and fines of thousands of pounds for rules they have not broken, is utterly indefensible.”
The Advantage Travel Partnership, which represents independent travel agents, said British travellers were being penalised for a chaotic system.

Its CEO, Julia Lo Bue-Said, said: “Travellers should not be penalised for failures in a system that is entirely outside their control. There needs to be greater accountability, alongside a straightforward process to challenge and correct inaccurate records.”

The Foreign Office said the problem was concerning. A spokesperson said: “We are aware of reports of inaccuracies in some EES records affecting British nationals, including incomplete records and the registration of some individuals who are exempt from EES. We are raising these issues as part of our engagement with the European Commission.”
It advised travellers to carry evidence of when they last left the EU and to raise any anomalies with border officials.
Travellers can check how many days of their allowance they have left by typing their passport number into the EES website. This records all visits to the Schengen zone since 10 April 2026.

If there is an unexpected shortfall, they can ask to have their record corrected before travelling by selecting the last country they visited on the Travel to Europe data protection page and contacting the relevant data controller.
Moyes said her efforts to do this have so far been in vain.

“In the last two weeks, I’ve tried every possible avenue,” she said. “I have now engaged an immigration lawyer, but not everyone is lucky enough to be able to afford this remedy. I have no idea how much time they think I have spent in Europe, and no idea whether I am safe to travel.”
The European Commission has been contacted for a comment.

articles.title: India news: New Delhi ready to mediate Black Sea food corridors, says Ukraine's Zelenskyy
articles.summary: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he discussed establishing "food corridors" in the Black Sea in a phone call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. DW has the latest.

image.caption: India's longstanding position on the Ukraine war has been that of a resolution through dialogue and diplomacy.Image: Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/Handout/EPA

blocks.text: Live
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he discussed establishing "food corridors" in the Black Sea in a phone call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. DW has the latest.
Prefer DW on Google

blocks.caption: India's longstanding position on the Ukraine war has been that of a resolution through dialogue and diplomacy.Image: Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/Handout/EPA

blocks.text: What you need to know
Here are the latest developments from India on Tuesday, November 10:

items: The leaders of India and Ukraine spoke over the phone ahead of a new round of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the United States.
Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said India was willing to help set up food corridors amid Black Sea attacks
India's Modi conveyed readiness to contribute to all efforts that are aimed at a peaceful resolution

blocks.text: November 10, 2026
Ukraine President Zelenskyy and Indian PM Modi speak ahead of Ukraine-Russia talks

India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy have held a telephonic conversation, with the Ukrainian leader saying that a discussion took place on Russia's attacks blocking grain exports in the Black Sea.
"India is ready to mediate in establishing corridors for grain exports in the Black Sea, blocked ​by Russian ⁠attacks," Zelenskyy wrote on X following the Monday evening call with Modi.
Modi and India's foreign ministry did not make a mention of the proposed food corridors in the official statements on the talks between the two leaders.
But Modi said he reiterated New Delhi's "firm commitment to contributing in every possible way towards a peaceful resolution."
India's diplomatic outreach in Ukraine war
In September, during a visit to Ukraine's capital Kyiv, Indian Foreign minister S Jaishankar offered to help end the Russia-Ukraine war.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha later said that his country had received four international truce proposals, including from India, which he described as the "most comprehensive."
Sybiha said Kyiv was ready to consider an energy and Black Sea ceasefire.
India's longstanding position on the Ukraine war has been that of a resolution through dialogue and diplomacy.
India has also continued its close economic relationship with decades-long partner Russia since the start of the war in 2022.
In October, Jaishankar first signalled that India had "got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy."

"We have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard. We are trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue, but going beyond that to cover some immediate concerns which both of them have on grain exports, on energy exports, on non-attack possibilities," he said at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi.
India also holds talks with Russia
Meanwhile, Monday's phone call between Zelenskyy and Modi came as negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States return to trilateral talks after months.
The fourth round of talks, starting Tuesday in United Arab Emirates' Abu Dhabi, comes after previous talks made no headway, with territorial and security guarantees being the major sticking points.
Zelenskyy said he had spoken to Modi about the latest diplomatic developments.
"The Prime Minister has said more than once, including directly to the Russian leader, ​that now is the time to end the war, not to continue it," ⁠Zelenskiy ​said, referring to the Indian leader.
Shortly after talks between Modi and Zelenskyy, Jaishankar announced that he spoke to the Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
"Our conversation focused on the Ukraine conflict and ongoing diplomatic initiatives." the Indian foreign minister said.
How India has become Russia's trade lifeline

articles.title: Oxford museum returns ancestral Naga skulls to India
articles.summary: The remains will be taken to Nagaland, where tribal leaders plan a joint memorial and burial.

blocks.text: The Pitt Rivers Museum holds more than 6,000 objects associated with Naga culture, believed to be the largest such collection in the world. Most were acquired during British colonial rule in India and Myanmar (the former Burma).
The museum's website lists 219 items as human remains.
These were added to the museum's collection between 1910 and 1940 and mostly collected by two colonial administrators who were anthropologists.
The museum's website, external mentions that the objects collected during this period were "frequently confiscated during punitive military expeditions, rather than freely given".
During their visit to Oxford, the Naga delegation also met descendants of one of the anthropologists involved in collecting the remains.
"The manner in which these human remains were taken away from our land leaves much for us to speculate," one of the tribal leaders, Thejao Vihienuo, told AFP.
"I suspect that nobody would have given the skull of his father or his grandfather as a gift to another person."
Anthropologists say that the Naga people once practised head hunting, severing the heads of enemies as trophies. But they also kept the heads of their own chiefs at the centre of villages.
The Pitt Rivers Museum, founded in the 19th Century, has previously returned human remains to indigenous communities in Australia, New Zealand and the US.
The latest handover to India concerns only the 39 ancestral remains and comes after a visit by a Naga delegation to Oxford in 2025, when it formally requested their return.
The museum had announced in September that the remains would be returned to India.

articles.title: Australia to introduce mandatory reporting after OpenAI hack to combat artificial intelligence ‘going rogue’
articles.summary:
Government flags criminal law changes to ensure companies can’t argue in future ‘that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded’

  • Get our

blocks.text: OpenAI will not face criminal penalties over the Medicare data breach, but the prime minister has flagged changes to Australia’s criminal law to crack down on future breaches by artificial intelligence companies.

Anthony Albanese on Tuesday released the recommendations of a “rapid review” into the June breach of a Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia, but not the findings or the report itself, which he committed to releasing in the future.

A key recommendation is for the Attorney-General’s Department, Australian Federal Police and Department of Home Affairs to consider introducing “penalties for egregious regulatory non-compliance” and a “failure to prevent” offence, which would criminalise developing an AI model that engaged in harmful conduct while failing “to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm”.

The rapid review came in response to an AI agent, developed by OpenAI, accessing data from Services Australia and three other systems in June. The company did not notify the Australian government until mid-September despite becoming aware of the incident itself in August, prompting criticism from Labor and Albanese.
Guardian Australia revealed last month OpenAI used AI to help write the email to notify Australian authorities.
Albanese said the government would set up a new AI safety regulator and implement six key obligations on AI companies:

items: Maintaining security controls across all stages of development and deployment.
Identifying and managing serious risks associated with their models.
Providing mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian government rapidly.
Allowing independent evaluation of their models.
Maintaining and publishing safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency.
Responding to updated standards and rules as technologies change.

blocks.text: The review recommended the federal government “consider mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting”, including around AI agents behaving in ways their creators may not have intended.

blocks.caption: Mandatory AI safety and security protections announced after OpenAI breach of Medicare – video

blocks.text: The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, appearing with Albanese, told reporters: “It should never be the case that there’s an argument that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded.
“We need to make sure that our laws and our systems keep pace with the technology and also make sure that we’re able to use the technology to find vulnerabilities before others do,” Burke said.
“The mandatory reporting, when artificial intelligence goes rogue, gives us a chance to be able to make sure that when this happens, the reporting occurs and occurs immediately.”

But despite the government’s earlier public anger at OpenAI, Albanese on Tuesday characterised OpenAI’s breach of Services Australia as “minor” in terms of the implications for personal privacy. Guardian Australia understands OpenAI is unlikely to face further legal proceedings related to the June breach.

While Albanese did not directly answer a question about whether the OpenAI incident in June would have breached the proposed new laws if they were in place, government sources indicated that the new legislation would address similar future incidents.
“The clear indication is that no information was got that involves people’s personal details,” Albanese said.
“All of that was confirmed essentially … but that doesn’t mean that it wasn’t a serious issue and that in other areas there might be more serious implications.”
after newsletter promotion
In a statement, an OpenAI spokesperson said the company was reviewing the recommendations and the government’s proposals.
“We have been in close dialogue with the Government and we’ll continue to engage constructively as it develops its proposed legislation,” they said.
A separate OpenAI-led process, which is discussing better coordination between AI developers and the government, is expected to report back by 31 December.
The review made 18 recommendations. Albanese said “we accept all of the recommendations and we’ve commenced work to implement them”.
The AI researcher Toby Walsh said the people in charge of these companies needed to be criminally liable to ensure they did the right thing.
“We’ve tried fining them, and we’re not the only ones. These companies are incredibly wealthy, and it’s almost impossible to fine them enough,” he told Guardian Australia.

But the Greens leader, David Shoebridge, branded the news a “capitulation” to the AI industry, claiming the reforms would not do enough to change the behaviour of those companies. He said the government should have committed to implementing even stronger changes, rather than the review’s recommendation that Labor simply “consider” them.
“Safety keeps coming second to corporate investment, and this review locks that priority in by tying every AI safety effort to bringing in more AI money and more datacentres,” Shoebridge claimed.

“Being a world leader in AI doesn’t mean being a doormat to big tech. It means being prepared to regulate it, to protect Australians and to make sure corporate profits don’t come at the expense of everyone else.”

The shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, said the Coalition backed the announcement, and had no criticism of the government. He said “AI is too important to become an unnecessarily partisan political contest”, signalling an “enduring and multi-partisan approach” to the technology.

articles.title: New Knesset speaker could be key to ousting Netanyahu as Israel’s PM
articles.summary:
Opposition politicians get first chance to take control of levers of power, even as they struggle to form government

Israel’s new Knesset will be sworn in on Tuesday, giving opposition…
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison Chief Middle East correspondent

blocks.text: Israel’s new Knesset will be sworn in on Tuesday, giving opposition politicians their first chance to take control of some levers of power, even as they struggle to form a new government to unseat Benjamin Netanyahu.
High on the agenda will be replacing the speaker, who wields immense influence by controlling the legislature’s agenda. The role is currently held by Amir Ohana, a close ally of Netanyahu.
Gadi Eisenkot, the former Israeli military chief who got the presidential mandate to try to form a coalition government at the weekend, may take the role himself, Israeli media reported on Monday.

The effort to wrest away control of the Knesset is significant enough that more than 160 top former security officials, including heads of the military, intelligence and police, warned that rightwing activists were planning to disrupt the day with violent attacks.

“Actors who oppose replacing the Knesset speaker intend to go to the Knesset on the day of the swearing-in ceremony and to prevent the MKs and their family members from entering the building,” a forum of retired commanders, the Democracy’s Protective Wall, warned in a letter to serving security chiefs.
“These same actors are encouraging tens of thousands of citizens who support their stance to come and to help them with their mission,” Ma’ariv newspaper quoted the letter saying.
If Eisenkot does not take the speaker role, opposition parties have agreed that someone from his Yashar party will be the nominee.

The opposition parties hold 67 seats in the 120-seat legislature, enough to install a consensus choice for speaker. All have described the current prime minister as a threat to the state and are keen to start moving against him, despite divides blocking the formation of a coalition.

But several of the Jewish-Israeli opposition parties in his “change” bloc have sworn not to sit with the Palestinian-led parties that hold over a quarter of the bloc’s seats, or even join a minority government that has their backing.
Eisenkot has vowed to broker a national emergency government, promising to achieve it with “creative and unconventional political acts”.
In a sign of challenges ahead, he effectively warned that some election promises would have to be broken to unseat Netanyahu.
“No one will be able to fulfil all the [campaign] promises they made, and all of us will need to compromise. That is also leadership, to know when to decide and set priorities,” he said.
There have been protests across Israel urging Jewish-Israeli opposition parties to put unseating Netanyahu ahead of a racist commitment to excluding Palestinian-led parties from government.

Palestinian citizens of Israel make up about 20% of Israel’s population and voted in unprecedented numbers this year, giving them 19 seats. Without them, the opposition bloc has fewer seats than Netanyahu’s diminished coalition.

Rightwing opposition leader Avigdor Lieberman has been trying to seek an alternative path to government through an alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties. They have long been Netanyahu allies but have been frustrated by his failure to deliver on the promise to pass broad military draft exemptions for their community into law. Lieberman has campaigned hard for universal conscription, but appears to prefer compromise on this issue to working with Palestinians.
“Has the End of Times arrived?” leading Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) journalist Arye Erlich wrote in a column for Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper.

“Has Avigdor Lieberman … the biggest persecutor of Haredim Israeli politics has seen in decades, suddenly come to believe that he can compromise on a military draft bill and sit in a coalition government alongside the Haredim?”

Even if Eisenkot does broker a coalition deal, he may delay announcing it until Netanyahu’s speaker has been replaced. Netanyahu is a master of political survival and last-minute deals, fracturing past coalitions by luring defectors into his own alliance.
Ohana could delay signing in a new government for up to a week, and some of the opposition do not want to give Netanyahu that much time to attack the pressure points of any fragile deal.

If Eisenkot cannot form a government, the mandate is passed to other leaders and if they too fail Israel must hold elections again. In the meantime Netanyahu and his far-right allies would stay on as a caretaker government.
Although Netanyahu is calling for his opponents to join him in a unity government, a long period of limbo followed by a new vote offers him a likelier path back to power.
If an alternative government takes power, it will be harder for Netanyahu to destabilise it, said Gideon Rahat, chair in political science at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
“Once they establish a government, they might be a minority government, it might be hard for them to do things, but nevertheless, they will be governing and it would be hard to oust them.”

articles.title: EU manufacturers could give up on competing with China by 2030, warns commerce chief
articles.summary:
Jens Eskelund says Europe may need to allow its companies to become part of Chinese firms’ supply chains

Europe’s manufacturers could give up on attempting to compete with their Chinese…

blocks.text: Europe’s manufacturers could give up on attempting to compete with their Chinese counterparts by the end of the decade if current trends continue amid fears over mass job losses, the head of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China has warned.

In a case of “if you can’t beat them, join them”, Jens Eskelund said European companies operating in China were now thinking “Made in China for China” could be replaced by a philosophy of “Made in China for the world”.

Eskelund, who heads the influential Beijing-headquartered body, said European manufacturers could find themselves at an existential crossroads by the end of the decade, asking themselves: “What is the point of trading?”

blocks.caption: The China import expo in Shanghai last week highlighted the latest five-year plan with the slogan: ‘New advances for a bright, win-win future’. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

blocks.text: As the EU gets tough with China with a deficit running at a record £1bn (€1.18bn) a day and an increasing mood for protectionism in Brussels, Berlin and Paris, he said European countries might need to shift their policies to allow domestic manufacturers to become part of Chinese firms’ supply chains, rather than treat them as competitors.

Eskelund, who is also a managing director of the shipping group Maersk’s Chinese operations, pointed to a report by Goldman Sachs that forecasted Chinese exports would lower the EU’s gross domestic product by 0.5% by the end of the decade while reducing Germany’s by up to 0.9%.
“It raises the question, if China’s trade delivers negative value, why trade?” the Danish businessman said.

blocks.caption: Jens Eskelund said European manufacturers could find themselves at an existential crossroads by the end of the decade. Photograph: Lisa O’Carroll

blocks.text: “If you are suddenly in a situation where trade creates a lot of value for one party, but it destroys value for the other, countries will begin to ask themselves, why do we trade?” he said, pointing to a potential doomsday scenario in which manufacturing disappeared from European countries, causing mass job losses, collapse in the tax base and potential multigenerational unemployment and spiralling social benefits costs.
Speaking in Brussels, where he has been in back-to-back meetings with European Commission officials to give them feedback from Beijing, he said Europe is at an inflection point.
“If we create new dependencies, ultimately that might result in Europe losing its ability to determine its own future,” with mass job losses and fraying of communities, Eskelund added.

That existential threat is already beginning to bite in Europe’s car, chemicals and renewable energy sectors, with the German automotive industry hit by a double whammy of reduced profits in China and cheap competition at home from Chinese companies such as BYD, Geely and SAIC Motor. Last week, BMW said its sales in China had dropped 22% in the first nine months of the year, in line with expectations of suppressed domestic demand, while issuing a second profit warning this year.

blocks.caption: Visitors watch a humanoid robot band perform at an expo in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province. Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Eskelund is not a fan of the term “China shock 2.0” – which refers to the impact of the huge rise in exports of, cars, chemicals and components – on local industry to the EU in the last five years. He said it should not have come as a surprise as Beijing’s plans to displace imports were the enduring theme of the last three five-year plans since Beijing’s Made in China strategy was agreed in 2015.

“I don’t really like the term China shock 2.0 because these things that are happening should not be a shock because it is all written in their five-year plans so you should be able to anticipate that,” Eskelund said.
“The proof of concept here is that China has been laser-focused on reducing its own dependencies over the last 30 years,” he added, pointing to a concomitant reduction in imports.

A recent report by Centre for European Reform (CER) urged Germany to stop “admiring” Beijing and change its strategy, with China’s latest five-year plan (2026 to 2030) a doubling-down on “self-reliance”.
“It is committed to displacing imports in the few sectors where it still depends on foreign supply,” said the CER.

blocks.caption: Workers paint wind turbine blades at a factory of Guodian United Power in Baoding, Hebei province. Photograph: Alexander F Yuan/AP

blocks.text: The sectors that have been identified in China’s latest five-year plan are AI, quantum computing; robotics; smart and green tech; biomanufacturing; brain-computer interfaces; and 6G communications.
Solar panels, wind turbines, robots, driverless cars, advanced chips are part of China’s new strategy for global domination.

Eskelund’s advice to those industries in Europe is not to hide but brace themselves for China to deliver. Once a strategy is decided in Beijing, incentives, tax breaksand subsidies flow down by region to town and village levels. Officials across the country know what to focus on and do, he said.
after newsletter promotion
His advice to EU leaders: “Engage with China and discuss getting to a point where everyone can see value is being created for both sides”, something he thinks Beijing understands.
While this might be an obvious point, Eskelund said a fundamental shift in approach was needed in Europe.

“China has always been very focused on outcomes, whereas Europe has been more focused on principles. It raises the question of whether following principles is delivering undesirable outcomes,” Eskelund said.

A view expressed in some quarters, including the UK, that trade imbalance could be addressed by increasing exports was just “fantasy”, said Eskelund, with this year’s surplus against the rest of the world expected to surpass 2025’s record $1.2tn (£900bn).

Eskelund said many companies were still making good money in China but the brutal competition in the country’s supply chains, combined with a currency undervalued by about 30%, left Europeans in the dust.
“What we see right now is that in almost all industrial verticals, almost anywhere in the world, you would have one and probably several Chinese competitors” he said.
“It’s just very, very difficult in most industries to compete with the Chinese.”

blocks.caption: An e-commerce warehouse in Jinhua City,  Zhejiang province.  Photograph: REX/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Giving up on trade is not the answer. If you can’t beat them join them. And that is what is now happening, the chamber has found.
“One way that they can compete with the Chinese supply chain is to become a part of the Chinese supply chain itself,” Eskelund said.
“For many companies it’s not the profit that you make in China that matters as much as the way Chinese supply chains enable you to compete on a global marketplace.”
This could mean making the products in China in joint domestic partnerships with European companies and getting into global supply chains in conjunction with Chinese firms.

“It is a sort of evolution from the old days when you came to China to service the Chinese market in China for China. It has now become: be in China, for the world. I think it’s a fairly significant shift,” Eskelund said.
For many of his members this had led to an “uptick in confidence” in the past year.
“This has turned out to be one of the ways that companies adapt, faced with a saturated market in China, they begin to explore exports,” he said.

articles.title: Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health
articles.summary: More than 2 billion people worldwide suffer from nutrient deficiencies, most of them in the Global South. The health consequences can be devastating.

image.caption: Fast food is typically calorie-rich, but low in nutritional valueImage: Christoph Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).
The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.

"In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president. "You could have a severe vitamin D deficiency for months before any symptoms appear at all. The same applies for vitamin B12. By the time symptoms appear, such as nerve damage, it's already too late."

A long-term B12 deficiency can damage the spinal cord, leading to numbness in the limbs, muscle weakness or even paralysis. Less common deficiency-related brain damage can cause memory loss and mental health issues.
Undernutrition vs. malnutrition
All B vitamins play an important role in metabolism, blood formation and healthy nerve function.

Vitamins, along with various minerals such as calcium, magnesium, iron, iodine and zinc, are classed as micronutrients. The body needs to source them from food, as it cannot produce them itself. Our bodies also need macronutrients like carbohydrates, carbohydrates, protein and fats that provide us with energy.

If the body consumes less food than it needs to maintain all bodily functions over a prolonged period of time, then this is known as undernutrition. A recent World Food Organization (FAO) report estimates that approximately 645 million people worldwide suffer from chronic undernutrition.

Malnutrition, on the other hand, occurs when we consume enough calories but lack certain macronutrients or micronutrients in our food. This, too, can make one sick over time and even prove fatal. About 2 billion people worldwide suffer from this so-called hidden hunger, most of them in the Global South. That said, even some people in industrialized nations lack important micronutrients in their nutrition.

blocks.caption: Golden rice, seen left, is genetically engineered to combat vitamin A deficiencyImage: Universität Freiburg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: One study, for instance, found that just under three-quarters of the US population did not meet the recommended daily intake of vitamin D between 2007 and 2010, with more than two-thirds falling short of the recommended amount of vitamin E. And in Germany, about one-third of the population suffered from vitamin D deficiency in 2017, according to the German Nutrition Society. Such deficiency can cause bone, joint and muscle pain. It may also lead to an increased risk of falls and bone fractures.

About one-third of Germans also had an insufficient intake of iodine, a trace element that is indispensable for the production of thyroid hormones. Iodine deficiency can therefore disrupt normal thyroid function. Not only that — during pregnancy, a baby's brain and nervous system can only properly develop with an adequate supply of iodine.

The cultivation of agricultural produce with partially long shelf life or high yields has in some cases caused a decrease in the micronutrient content of fruits, vegetables and grains. Whether this drop in micronutrients is impacting human health, however, is a matter of debate.
Empty calories

Malnutrition can result from an unbalanced diet that, while filling and providing energy, lacks essential micronutrients. Examples of such empty calories include fast food and highly processed foods, as well as white bread and white rice.
Poverty is often the reason for such an unbalanced diet, for example when people in the Global South can only afford to buy staples such as flour or rice.
Another study found that in Germany, households at risk of poverty are more likely to consume foods that are low in nutrients and high in calories.

Depression is also associated with an increased risk of nutrient deficiency. "People often lose their appetite, and when they neglect their self-care, they may end up eating a very unbalanced diet," Pirlich told DW. His research shows that older adults and people who live alone often develop malnutrition, too. The risk also increases the more medications a person takes.

Many diseases result in the body being less efficient at absorbing or utilizing nutrients through the intestines. This applies to people with inflammatory or chronic disease, such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease, liver disease and cancer.
Malnutrition and hospital care

The DGEM estimates that some 30% of all patients receiving inpatient care in Germany are affected by or at risk of malnutrition. Yet health insurance data shows that only about 1% of patients are screened and treated for nutrient deficiencies.

Often, patients' malnutrition worsens during their hospital stay. The consequences can be serious, potentially causing additional complications, delayed recuperation, longer hospital stays and even increased mortality rates. This results in higher healthcare expenditure, amounting to billions each year.

German policymakers and medical associations are therefore developing a plan to better screen for and treat malnutrition in hospitals. The road map will be ready by 2027 and copy the Dutch approach in the sense that all patients are checked for nutritional deficiencies upon hospital admission.

blocks.caption: Elderly people are at higher risk of malnutritionImage: Karl-Josef Hildenbrand/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: How can we avoid nutrient deficiency?
Pirlich wants to see such screenings for at-risk groups in outpatient clinics, too: "This includes all those with chronic and serious illnesses and, above all, older adults."
To prevent poverty-related malnutrition, Pirlich suggests increased access to healthy food, offering free school meals as an example.

The nutritional expert recommends eating a diet that is varied and largely plant-based. "Secondary plant compounds have a very positive effect, and if you eat a highly diverse diet, you consume many different foods that are [nutritionally] beneficial," said Pirlich.
There's a simple rule of thumb: The more colorful your food, the better.

Also, cook vegetables as gently as possible, because overheating and keeping them warm for too long destroys their vitamins. Long storage periods also lead to vitamin loss, so it makes sense to go for seasonal and regional foods in particular.
But even when ensuring a healthy and balanced diet, some people still develop a nutrient deficiency. A blood test can provide clarity, and dietary supplements may help make up for the deficiency.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Polish unity on show in silent march to honour Krakow shooting victims
articles.summary: Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by Saturday's attack, writes Sarah Rainsford.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Thousands gathered at Krakow's historic Market Square to honour the victims of Saturday's attack
BySarah Rainsford
Southern and Eastern Europe correspondentReporting fromKrakow
Thousands of people joined a silent march through central Krakow on Monday night, in memory of those killed and injured when a gunman went on a violent rampage at the weekend.
The crowd were led by Poland's president and prime minister, the bitter political rivals putting on a rare show of unity after the country's deadliest attack in modern times.
As they reached the historic Market Square, a bugler played from the tower.
Many people were carrying flowers or candles to leave at the shrines that now dot the cobblestones, one marking each spot where someone died.
Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by this attack. It has left people struggling to make some kind of sense of what happened.
The alleged gunman has been named as 24-year-old Michal Oksinski by local media.
Critically injured in a shoot-out with police, he did not regain consciousness and died in hospital early on Monday.
Initially, the interior minister claimed that Oksinski was driven by far-right, extremist views. The national prosecutor's office now says that it's too soon to say he was "inspired" by any ideology.

"The minister wanted to win domestic political points. That's not responsible behaviour," Dr Pawel Musialek of the Jagiellonian University suggests, in a country where politics is highly - and often viciously - polarised.
"So far we've seen no clear message that this guy was strongly ideological, and that it's not more like something from the darknet."

There's been no mention of any letter or manifesto that Oksinski left. One neighbour told Polish news site Onet that the 24-year-old was a "bit of a loner" but few who knew him well have spoken publicly.
In addition to his electronic devices like his phone, investigators are examining a number of badges that Oksinski had attached to his military-style outfit.

The prosecutor's office says a yellow Gadsden flag with a coiled snake symbol was displayed in his bedroom. "It has various meanings of freedom and rebellion," a spokesman emphasised. "Not necessarily negative."
It was at Oksinski's home that the bodies of his parents and sister were discovered.
It's alleged that he shot them, before driving some 200km (125 miles) south to continue the killing in Krakow.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Candles and flowers have been placed around the square in places where someone died

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Candles and flowers have been placed around the square in places where someone died
Two days on, shops and cafes around the market square are beginning to fill up again, but the mood is subdued.
A Zara clothes shop is still boarded up, after bullets smashed the glass. A local man in his 50s died just outside.
Jo, a Scottish tourist, saw paramedics "who got there ridiculously fast", fighting to save him. "It was all pretty grim."
Like many, she initially mistook the rifle shots for fireworks.
On the opposite corner of the square, beside another cluster of flowers, people keep pausing to take pictures of the holes that were blasted into the wall by gunfire.
One of the six victims has been identified as a Polish painter in her 50s, who was a mother of four, and in town with friends for an exhibition opening.
A British citizen and an Austrian who died are yet to be named publicly.
Several drivers of the horse-drawn carriages that are usually poised to trot tourists around the square were seriously injured.

blocks.caption: Image caption, "This is supposed to be a safe place!" Olha, a Ukrainian citizen, moved to Krakow for safety when Russia launched its full-scale invasion

blocks.text: "This is supposed to be a safe place!" Olha, a Ukrainian citizen, moved to Krakow for safety when Russia launched its full-scale invasion
Olha, who works in a nearby chocolate shop says everyone is now nervous.
On Saturday, people rushed into her store to escape the gunman who was tearing around in his car, firing through the window.
Olha is Ukrainian, and moved to Krakow when Russia invaded. "We left our own country for safety. This is supposed to be a safe place!" she exclaimed.
"It's so sad, and so scary. Especially that he drove all the way here for two hours, planning this and thinking about it."
She regrets that the gunman did not survive: "So many are dead, so many lives have been ruined, and now there will be no justice."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Political differences were set aside between President Karol Nawrocki (left) and Prime Minister Donald Tusk (right) at the vigil on Monday

blocks.text: Image source, Filip Radwanski/Anadolu via Getty Images
Political differences were set aside between President Karol Nawrocki (left) and Prime Minister Donald Tusk (right) at the vigil on Monday
When Oksinski's car was searched, four firearms and "hundreds of rounds of ammunition" were found, all owned legally by the alleged killer and his father.
Both were members of the Swit Starachowice sports club, where there is a shooting range. A spokesman recalls Michal Oksinski as unremarkable: average competition results and normal behaviour.
He had been just three times this year, most recently in August with his father. The club spokesman is adamant that it does not train combat firing, only shooting from a fixed point.
Gun ownership in Poland has grown considerably since war broke out in Ukraine just across the border, but this is the first mass shooting anyone here can remember.
Inevitably, it has brought scrutiny of the checks over who qualifies to handle such weapons, including psychological tests, as Michal Oksinski passed all of them.
On Monday, the government announced an urgent review.

blocks.caption: Image caption, "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon"

blocks.text: "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon"
At the spot where Oksinski's car was intercepted and he was shot by police there is another memorial, this one in honour of the officers still in hospital.
Some have brought flowers, but a girl called Bianka has left a card that reads: "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon."
A couple of steps away, there's a series of bullet holes in the glass.
"This man was a real hero, he didn't hesitate," Ania says, referring to officer Jakub Kulik who was shot in the chest. His condition remains serious. "We're here to help him fight for his life."
"Nothing like this has never happened before, it's terrible," a young man called Wojtek tells me.
He's only glad that the gunman responsible for such horror turned out to be Polish.
"People here are already against immigration, so that would have been even worse."
Ania thinks Poles will pull through, though the country's image as a low-crime oasis has been shattered.
Most of all, she's angry that Michal Oksinski died without accounting for the devastation he allegedly wrought.
"I think we deserve to know why."

articles.title: Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
articles.summary: AI safety regulator will also be created after a rogue OpenAI agent hacked government websites.

blocks.text: Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.

In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.
On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.
AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".
"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.
One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .
This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".
The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.
This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.
In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.
OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.
It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.
Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident" and with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.
Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

articles.title: Mortgage holders’ confidence crashes to lowest level since 1994 as year that ‘feels like a recession’ looms
articles.summary:
Westpac survey results signal growing sense of ‘helplessness’ while Jim Chalmers faces growing pressure to rein in spending

Confidence among mortgaged households has crashed to its lowest…

blocks.text: Confidence among mortgaged households has crashed to its lowest level in more than three decades amid a growing sense of “helplessness” about the economy, even as a dramatic shift in financial markets suggests there is now a strong chance of a Reserve Bank rate cut by this time next year.
The latest Westpac survey showed its consumer sentiment index sinking again in November to reach a four-year low, amid deepening pessimism about the near-term prospects for the economy.
As Labor comes under increasing pressure over persistent cost-of-living pressures, the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, played down tensions with the treasurer, Jim Chalmers.
A day after the frontbencher Murray Watt called for colleagues to stop undermining Chalmers, Albanese said: “The treasurer is doing a great job”.
The PM said he was working closely with Chalmers in the lead-up to next month’s mid-year budget update, which will include cuts to government spending as pressure mounts to contain inflation.
“This is a treasurer who’s produced a couple of budget surpluses, lower deficits, [who is] producing economic reform,” Albanese said.

Matthew Hassan, Westpac’s head of economic forecasting, said the mood among households was last this bad in 2022, when inflation was running close to 8% and after the RBA had lifted borrowing costs by 4 percentage points over the previous year.

“Prior to that, readings this weak had only ever been seen in the economy’s darkest moments: at the onset of the Covid pandemic; the height of the GFC; and during the recessions in the early 1990s and early 1980s,” Hassan said.
Hassan said while the economic backdrop was not as extreme now as it was during the pandemic and its immediate aftermath, there were “shades of Covid in the responses” from households.
Confidence in the economic outlook over the coming year reached its weakest since August 2020, the survey showed, matching a low point last recorded during the pandemic.
“The comparison with August 2020 is quite useful as that was when Melbourne went into its second lockdown and just before the government massively scaled up income support,” Hassan said.

“There was a sense of helplessness at that stage; there was nothing we could do to avoid the pandemic, and there was nothing the government could do [to avoid the pandemic]. Obviously when the jobkeeper measures were put in place that comforted a lot of people.

“There is a similar feeling of helplessness now. You can argue a substantial portion of what is happening is out of our control, such as rising fuel prices, and there’s only so much the authorities can do to cushion Australians from that impact.”
Indebted households were gloomier still, the survey showed, with pessimism among this group at its worst in records stretching back to 1994.

The latest survey comes a week after Michele Bullock, the RBA governor, warned that the year ahead would “feel like it’s a recession” thanks to persistent cost-of-living pressures alongside weak economic growth.
After five rate increases this year, nearly three in four respondents said they expected another rate hike over the coming 12 months.
Even as the mood in the community darkens, financial markets have begun factoring in the chance of lower interest rates from the middle of next year.
The implied probability of an RBA rate cut was more than 50% by August next year, according to ANZ data, and a decrease to 4.6% was fully priced in by December 2027.
Investors have been rethinking their forecasts for central bank moves alongside a rapid retreat in the global oil price.
After testing a post-Iran war high of nearly US$118 a barrel at the end of October, the global benchmark, Brent crude, has plunged by 20% to below US$94.
“Our base case is that rates do start to come down from August next year, and we don’t see any further hikes,” Hassan said.
– Additional reporting by Tom McIlroy

articles.title: US officials seek ‘final end’ to Russia-Ukraine war as Abu Dhabi talks begin
articles.summary:
First substantive peace talks since February to include US proposal for ‘long-term security architecture’ between Moscow and Europe

US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war…

blocks.text: US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday in the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February.
The talks are also the first since the US launched joint strikes with Israel against Iran, and they follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home.
Part of the Trump administration’s proposal involves drawing a new “long-term security architecture” between Russia and Europe, administration officials have said.

European officials are concerned that Russia may stick to its hardline demands that Nato should roll back its military footprint across eastern Europe, which would threaten to leave allies vulnerable to Moscow’s influence at a time of historic tensions with the west.

Since his first decade in power, Vladimir Putin has complained about Nato’s eastward expansion and sought to renegotiate the balance of power between Nato and Russia – but never before have those demands been embraced by a sitting US administration, which has made it clear that it is desperate to get to a deal.

Previewing the discussions, a US administration official said the US would “need Europe at the table” to end the war. He said negotiators could also revive the Nato-Russian council that was suspended after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and potentially lift sanctions against Russia to get to a deal.

The US officials also claimed that they had discussed with Russia potential security guarantees to Ukraine similar to Nato’s article 5, which protect member states in case of an attack. Russia has strongly opposed Nato admitting Ukraine or western countries placing troops in Ukraine.
“What they would be getting would be effectively very similar to Nato,” an administration official said.

“Getting a US security guarantee is a really, really big deal,” the official added, saying it would be up to Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy to discuss. “And if he wants to do that, that’s that’s a very, very big deal in terms of resources and funding and military support.”

Critics have expressed skepticism about what may trigger those security guarantees, however, noting that article 5 does not oblige Nato member states to defend others, and that cyber-attacks and other forms of hybrid warfare have blurred the line for what would require a military response.

Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a lead negotiator for the United States, described a potential new framework for European in general terms on Monday, saying the US would seek “stronger consultation, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, and reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, while fully respecting the sovereignty and independent decision-making of every nation”.

European delegations from Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and the European Union will meet US negotiators in Abu Dhabi to discuss the “long-term security architecture between Russia and Europe in order to figure out how to reduce future conflicts”.

A European security official from a country attending the talks said that the US proposal was not yet clear and that they were bracing themselves for the US to pose serious concessions to Russia during the Abu Dhabi consultations.

“We already have a European security architecture in place,” said Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s top diplomat, at a G7 foreign ministers meeting on Monday. “This includes international agreements under which Russia has undertaken obligations, including with regard to sovereignty and territorial integrity. The problem is that Russia is not respecting these agreements.”
Donald Trump has also said that Ukraine would like be expected to give up territory in a final deal, and would end with a “little bit different shape“.

Trump last week after meeting with Kremlin advisor Kirill Dmitriev said he would seek a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”. Critics are concerned that Trump and Putin could try to go over the heads of European leaders in order to negotiate a peace that gives serious concessions to Russia.

“There’s a lot of baggage that people in Europe have about this idea,” said a US administration official, pointing specifically to Russia’s 2021 proposal that was viewed as an ultimatum to Nato to get out of eastern Europe.

In 2021, Russia issued a list of demands to Nato that included a ban on expansion to new countries including Ukraine, a rollback of troops to its pre-1997 borders, and limits on where it could place missiles. Nato rejected that proposal and Russia invaded Ukraine less than a month later.

“We have to build something new that works today… Because if all the old architecture was working well, then we wouldn’t be in this long war. And so obviously something’s not working, and we need to come up with a way that when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war,” said the US administration official.
The content of those proposals are not clear yet, although the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, claimed on Monday “there’s been some advances made in what that architecture should look”.
“We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point,” he added.

articles.title: Duterte's SALNs list property in nonexistent Davao del Norte barangay
articles.summary: Second defense witness confirmed a mismatch between SALN and tax records on a lot in Samal, Davao del Norte.

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:56pm
Island Garden City of Samal Assessor John Kenneth Enumerables during the 41st day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Nov. 10, 2026.
Senate PRIB
MANILA, Philippines — A property declared by Vice President Sara Duterte in her asset disclosures is listed under a barangay that does not exist in Samal, Davao del Norte.

Samal Assessor John Kenneth Enumerables, the second defense witness, testified on Tuesday, November 10 that the property, covered by a transfer certificate of title ending in 3134, was listed under "Barangay Matanos" in Duterte's Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.
But the city's tax records place the property in Barangay San Isidro. Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero questioned the witness about the conflicting locations.
"May barangay po ba na Matanos sa Samal?" Escudero asked. ("Is there a barangay called Matanos in Samal?")
"Wala po," Enumerables replied. ("There is none.")
Escudero also asked whether the two locations were the same, which Enumerables denied.
The assessor explained that he had identified the property based on its assessed and market values.
Discrepancy traced to older title
Escudero then referred to the October 1 testimony of Marco Pineda, deputy Register of Deeds of Samal, who had previously addressed the property's location.
According to Escudero, Pineda testified that the Barangay Matanos address had been carried over from the property's mother title, the original land title from which subsequent titles were derived.
Escudero explained that under Presidential Decree 1529, the Register of Deeds cannot alter the original location details and must instead carry them over to subsequent titles.
Duterte's 2019 SALN listed a residential lot in Barangay Matanos, Kaputian District, Samal, with a reported acquisition cost of P4.04 million.
The property had an assessed value of P52,500 and was declared as acquired in 2013.
Prosecution counsel Benjamin Tolosa noted the property also appeared in Duterte's SALNs for 2020, 2021 and 2022.

articles.title: Australia to introduce mandatory AI safeguards
articles.summary: The Australian government's decision to establish an AI safety regulator comes after an OpenAI agent accessed a government medical statistics portal without authorization.

image.caption: OpenAI and rival Anthropic have agreed to meet the reporting requirements for data breaches that involve AI agentsImage: Jonathan Raa/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Australia will introduce mandatory safeguards for artificial intelligence companies, including compulsory reporting of security breaches and independent oversight of AI systems, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday.
The decision comes after an incident in which an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to a government medical statistics portal while researching public medical spending.

Albanese said his center-left Labor government had accepted all the review's recommendations, which include requiring AI companies to report misaligned behavior and cyber incidents. The government will also consider reforms to criminal law to address cases of serious misconduct.

The government plans to establish an AI safety regulator to oversee security controls during the development and deployment of AI systems, identify serious risks and conduct independent evaluations of models.
My AI therapist: A chatbot experiment
"The AI ⁠safety regulator will be ​able to enforce significant penalties for AI companies doing the wrong thing," Albanese said.
"The law needs to get ahead of, and in some cases, make sure that it catches up with what is a very fast-changing world," he told reporters.
AI breach stirred tension between Australia and US tech companies
OpenAI has said it learned of the breach in August and that the incident was unintentional. Its review found no evidence that the AI agent had accessed patient records.

Canberra declined to exempt ChatGPTmaker OpenAI and rival Anthropic from copyright laws for model ⁠training which would require them instead to negotiate licensing agreements with Australian rights ​holders.
Both companies told an Australian parliamentary committee last month that they would welcome mandatory reporting requirements for data breaches involving their AI agents.

articles.title: NAMFREL urges no more delays after SC ruling on BSKE
articles.summary: “Our concern is not the length of the term. It is how the term was lengthened. Congress may set a term, but only voters can grant a mandate,” the poll watchdog said in a statement.

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:43pm
Women cast their vote at Pasong Tamo Elementary School in Quezon City during the automated mock barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) elections on August 8, 2023.
STAR / Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — Election watchdog National Citizens’ Movement for Free Elections is warning against further delays to the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections after the Supreme Court declared constitutional a law extending barangay officials' terms and moving polls to 2028.
In a statement on Monday, November 9, the organization said that while it respected the High Court's decision, it has not "exhausted the ways the right to suffrage can be protected."
The group cited objections raised by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen and Associate Justice Antonio Kho on the law’s potential to impede the right to vote.

Leonen, joined by Associate Justices Ramon Paul Hernando and Ricardo Rosario, reasoned that successive extensions may "defer the vote unconstitutionally," and that the law prevented Filipinos ageing out of SK eligibility before 2028 from exercising their right to vote.
Kho, meanwhile, was joined by Associate Justice Alfredo Caguioa in saying that Congress could have adopted the new term while holding the elections as scheduled.
The 2028 cycle, Kho argued, created the overlap with the 2028 elections that the law claimed to avoid.
“Our concern is not the length of the term. It is how the term was lengthened. Congress may set a term, but only voters can grant a mandate,” the poll watchdog said in a statement.
The organization also emphasized the need for Congress to be proactive in future scenarios, saying it need not wait for another court case to reform election laws.
Passed in September 2026, Republic Act 12326 moved the next BSK elections from Nov. 2, 2026 to November 2028.
The law also fixes the terms of such officials at five years, effectively granting term extensions to officials voted in during the 2023 elections.

Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal challenged the constitutionality of the law, arguing that it failed to meet the guidelines of a 2023 ruling that allowed the postponement of elections “only for important, substantial or compelling reasons.”
Macalintal also argued that the law violated the people’s right to vote, as voters in 2023 elected the incumbent officials with the belief they would serve three-year terms.

articles.title: After witness' 'China' flip-flop, senator-judges warn vs lying under oath
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court warned witnesses that false testimony could lead to contempt and possible perjury cases.

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:32pm
MANILA, Philippines — Senator-judges warned witnesses in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial that false testimony could lead to contempt and perjury proceedings.

On Tuesday, November 10, Senator-judge Tito Sotto sought clarification from Presiding Officer Chiz Escudero on the penalties that could be imposed on witnesses caught lying before the impeachment court.

"We have penalties and sanctions against those who lie before the impeachment court. Will you please refresh my memory on this matter so that the witnesses and the prosecution and the defense will be reminded as well?" Sotto asked.
Escudero then said witnesses who lie under oath may be cited for contempt and could also face perjury complaints.

"They may be subject to contempt by the court, Your Honor, and in addition to that, may be subjected to cases of perjury should one be filed against him before the proper prosecutor's office and or courts of law, because the statements given by any witness is under oath and is therefore covered by our laws on perjury as well," Escudero said.
Senator-Judge Ping Lacson also stressed that the impeachment court's power to punish contempt is expressly provided under its rules and is not merely implied.
The reminder came a day after the testimony of Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin, the first witness presented by Duterte's defense, drew questions from senator-judges over his answers.

During Monday's hearing, senator-judges pressed Adalin after he initially said he could not recall details of a trip he supposedly made to China. He later acknowledged that he traveled there in January 2026 with Davao City officials.
Questions were also raised over his testimony concerning properties listed in Duterte's Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.
The properties are being examined under Article II of the impeachment complaint, which covers allegations of unexplained wealth and discrepancies in Duterte's asset declarations.

articles.title: DOJ seeks cyberlibel charges vs Topacio, 5 others
articles.summary: The Department of Justive has filed a resolution reversing its decision to junk a cyberlibel complaint filed by Sen. Risa Hontiveros against six social media personalities who accused the lawmaker of…

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:30pm

MANILA, Philippines — Cyberlibel charges have been recommended against lawyer Ferdinand Topacio and five other social media personalities following a Department of Justice resolution granting the review of a complaint filed by Sen. Risa Hontiveros that was dismissed in December 2025.

Though Hontiveros must tolerate criticism as a public official, the respondents “crossed the line separating protected criticism and opinion from the public and malicious imputation of specific, discreditable acts,” the resolution said.
Hontiveros welcomed the indictment of Topacio, Byron “Banat By” Cristobal, Jeffrey “Ka Eric” Celiz, Jose “Jay” Sonza, Krizette “Kiffy” Chu and Alex “Tio Moreno” Destor.
“Sinabi natin dati pa: hindi dapat palampasin ang mapanganib na kasinungalingan laban sa mga tumestigong biktima ng pang-aabuso ni Apollo Quiboloy,” the senator said.
(“We’ve said it before: lies directed at the victims who testified to the abuse committed by Apollo Quiboloy must not go unaddressed.”)

Hontiveros' complaint, filed in July 2025, stemmed from social media posts published by the personalities that accused her of bribing and coaching witnesses during the Senate investigation into sex trafficking allegations against Quiboloy.
The posts also alleged that Hontiveros launched “organized propaganda efforts” to discredit various public officials, including Vice President Sara Duterte and former President Rodrigo Duterte.

Hontiveros filed a similar complaint against Michael Maurillo, a former Kingdom of Jesus Christ member who claimed he was coerced by Hontiveros to give false testimony against Quiboloy and the Dutertes.
Murillo was indicted early 2026, with an arrest warrant issued against him by the Pasay Regional Trial Court Branch 111 in February.

Quiboloy, meanwhile, is detained at the Pasig City Jail for sexual abuse charges and qualified human trafficking. The DOJ is preparing to file a court petition to extradite the church leader as he also faces child sex trafficking and fraud charges in the US.

Criminal and libel complaints were filed by his camp against Hontiveros, Rep. Leila de Lima (Mamamayang Liberal) and Rep. Perci Cendaña (Akbayan) in September, over statements referring to him as a “sex offender."

articles.title: Duterte defense asks ICC to drop two witnesses, calls their accounts hearsay
articles.summary: Lawyers for former president Rodrigo Duterte have asked the International Criminal Court to remove two prosecution witnesses from his case, arguing that what they claim to know about his drug war…

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:16pm
Peter Haynes, president of the International Criminal Court Bar Association, speaks at the opening of the International Criminal Court's judicial year in February 2020.
ICCBA

MANILA, Philippines — Lawyers for former president Rodrigo Duterte have asked the International Criminal Court to remove two prosecution witnesses from his case, arguing that what they claim to know about his drug war comes mostly from rumor and hearsay.

In a filing dated November 9 and released in redacted form, lead defense counsel Peter Haynes said the witnesses, identified only as P-1334 and P-1348, were absent for nearly the entire period covered by the two counts under Duterte’s presidency.
As a result, the defense said, they could have “almost no direct knowledge” of how decisions were made or how operations were carried out.
The filing responds to an October 21 prosecution request to admit the witnesses’ earlier recorded statements without calling them to testify.
Prosecutors are arguing the two witnesses' statements will help prove the broader elements of crimes against humanity, particularly Duterte's alleged policy of “neutralizing” criminals.
Prosecutors are relying on Rule 68(2)(b) of the court’s rules, which lets judges admit prior recorded testimony from absent witnesses.
According to the defense's November 9 filing, P-1334 confirmed she had no personal knowledge of how Duterte allegedly passed instructions through former national police chief Bato dela Rosa.
"She never saw Dela Rosa do anything of the sort, and recognized that her account is based on stories she had heard," the filing read.
The defense also argues that "the little she claims to know about Incident 13 comes entirely from newspapers or 'people talking,'" the redacted filing read.
If the court decides to keep the two witnesses, the defense said it would not cross-examine them and would leave their admission to the judges’ discretion.
It asked, however, that the chamber disregard passages on Duterte’s own conduct, including allegations that specific orders to kill were issued and claims attributing certain funds to him.

Government figures put the number of people killed in police anti-drug operations under Duterte at more than 6,000, while human rights groups estimate the toll is several times higher. Duterte has consistently defended the campaign.
Duterte's trial opens November 30.
