articles.title: Iran war oil shock drives dip in global emissions, study shows
articles.summary: Global carbon emissions are expected to fall slightly in 2026, but not because of major progress on climate action. Instead, it's high energy prices following the US attack on Iran that's driving the…

image.caption: Carbon emissions are the main drivers of climate changeImage: Jason Whitman/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a new study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.
Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026.

"It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.
"So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons."
The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference.
No structural change yet

The study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%.
"A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned.
Turkey on the climate frontline

A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterwards, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters said. "What we see this year is oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%."
Emissions expected to rebound

It is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered.

While the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind, the temporary emissions reversal, there's also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves.
"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University.

And even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

articles.title: Who gave barangay execs 5 years? Supreme Court dissenters say not voters
articles.summary: The dissenters raised different arguments, from the lack of a compelling reason for the delay to the application of the longer term to officials already in office.

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 11:41am

MANILA, Philippines — Five Supreme Court justices warned that extending the terms of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) officials to five years and moving the elections to November 2028 improperly curtails the people's right to vote.

Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen and Associate Justices Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa, Ramon Paul Hernando, Ricardo Rosario and Antonio Kho Jr. dissented from the majority decision upholding the constitutionality of Republic Act 12326. Leonen, Caguioa and Kho issued separate opinions, with Hernando and Rosario joining Leonen's dissent.

The majority held that RA 12326 is primarily a term-setting law rather than an election-postponement measure and that Congress has the authority to determine the terms of barangay officials. It also found the November 2028 election schedule reasonable.
The decision, penned by then Associate Justice and now Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda, was promulgated on October 14 and released to the public on November 6.
Caguioa: No compelling reason for extension
Caguioa cautioned that allowing the law to stand would permit Congress to evade judicial review by packaging constitutionally questionable election postponements as term-setting measures.

"I register anew my strong dissent. The Court should not countenance, for a second time, a legislative maneuver that unduly curtails the people's right of suffrage. Republic Act No. 12326 must be declared unconstitutional," Caguioa said.
He also argued that no compelling government interest was shown to justify extending the terms of barangay and SK officials from four to five years so soon after the previous extension.

"If 'effective local governance' is the objective, what has changed in the past year to warrant yet another term extension? Without any study or evidence showing that the four-year term is inadequate or ineffective, the further extension to five years can only be described as whimsical and arbitrary and unduly lengthens the intervals between elections without any demonstrated necessity," Caguioa said.
Kho: Law also postpones elections

Kho argued that RA 12326 is not merely a term-setting law but also an election-postponement measure and should therefore have been subjected to the standards laid down by the Supreme Court in its 2023 Macalintal v. Comelec ruling.
Under that ruling, the postponement of elections must be supported by an important, substantial or compelling reason.
Kho said RA 12326 failed to present a sufficiently important or compelling justification for moving the elections to 2028.

"The postponement of the BSK elections to November 2028 is unreasonably long that the authority of the incumbents to discharge the functions of the office no longer continue to be based on the free expression of the will of the electorate," Kho said.
He also criticized the majority for declining to strike down the law.
"Verily, the Court must not remain passive. The Court should not shirk from its duty in declaring unconstitutional a law that evidently violates the Constitution," Kho said.

"In doing so, the Court will not claim to exercise authority over Congress. Far from it. It would be merely fulfilling its solemn duty to uphold the supremacy of the Constitution. This, the ponencia unfortunately blatantly fails to perform."
Leonen: New term should not apply to incumbents
Leonen, meanwhile, agreed that Congress has the authority to change the terms of barangay officials but said it cannot apply the new five-year term to incumbents elected under a shorter term.

"I regret that I cannot fully join the majority. Postponing the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections abuses the inherent sovereign right to suffrage. This undermines our democracy and the concept of a republican government," Leonen said.

"While the Constitution allows Congress to modify the terms of office of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials, it cannot, however, apply that change to incumbents. Otherwise, our right to suffrage will be infringed," he added.
Leonen likened the vote to a sacred covenant and a public act through which "sovereign" people, the voters, confer authority on officials for a defined period.

"Unlike a contract, which ordinarily arises from private agreement between parties, an election is a public act through which the sovereign people confer authority upon their chosen representatives," he said.

"Through this act, the electorate entrusts the exercise of governmental authority to particular officials for a period prescribed by law. In turn, the candidate elected assume office pursuant to the same legal framework," he added.

Leonen also raised concerns about the effect of the postponement on young voters and prospective SK candidates. Because SK membership and candidacy are subject to age limits, some who would have been eligible to participate in the November 2026 elections may no longer qualify by 2028.
He closed his opinion by urging the court to "do better and protect the sacred fundamental covenant of suffrage."
"We owe the people that much," Leonen said.

articles.title: Lula, a staunch Trump critic, to make first state visit during ASEAN
articles.summary: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will make a state visit to the Philippines on November 14 and 15, the first by a sitting Brazilian head of state, Malacañang said on…

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 11:30am

Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva speaks during a meeting of the National Council for the Industrialisation of Critical and Strategic Minerals at the Planalto Palace in Brasília on November 5, 2026.
AFP / Evaristo Sa

MANILA, Philippines — Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will make a state visit to the Philippines on November 14 and 15, the first by a sitting Brazilian head of state, Malacañang said on Tuesday, November 10.

Lula, who won a fourth term in Brazil's presidential runoff last month, will join the November 15 session of the 49th ASEAN Summit as "Guest of the Chair" at the invitation of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) said in a statement.
The Philippines, which holds the ASEAN chairship this year, will host leaders from the bloc and its partner countries in Metro Manila through November 18.

Marcos will receive Lula at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City, where the two leaders will hold bilateral talks on trade and investment, agriculture, energy, science and technology, defense and technical cooperation.
The agenda also includes closer coordination in multilateral forums and among developing economies of the so-called Global South.
The trip is one of Lula's first major foreign trips since the October runoff in which he defeated Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.

Brazil became ASEAN's first Latin American "sectoral dialogue partner" in August 2022, a tier lower than the full dialogue partnerships the bloc holds with powers such as the United States, China and Japan

Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro in August paid a courtesy call to Lula and Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira, in which both sides discussed bilateral agreements covering cooperation in energy and tourism, among others.
There is no official confirmation yet that Lula's visit will overlap with Trump, whose attendance at the main summit from November 16 to 18 was confirmed by Malacañang in October.
Trump has called Brazil's vote a disgrace and has questioned the result without offering evidence.

articles.title: Trump says Iran war is 'effectively over' militarily with further strikes unlikely
articles.summary: The president says the US is keeping "status quo" with Iran but remains “locked and loaded” should the situation in the Middle East change.

blocks.text: Donald Trump says the Iran war "militarily is effectively over" declaring that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East conflict.
"We're just keeping it the status quo," the US president said on Monday. "And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours."

Addressing reporters from the White House press briefing room, Trump said that renewed US attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" but that the US was "locked and loaded" should the circumstances change.
Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed doubts about the US president's prior comments about resolving the conflict.
Responding to a question over why he would not officially declare an end to the conflict, Trump said that some of the Gulf allies could still face Iranian aggression.
"We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they're not hurt," Trump said, suggesting that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports was helping to make the region more secure.
Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani in the Oval Office earlier on Monday, saying they had an "excellent conversation" about negotiations to end the war.
In a post on X, the Qatari prime minister said he held "positive discussions" with Trump and Vice-President JD Vance on "reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region".
Efforts to broker a peace between Washington and Tehran have largely been held indirectly through mediators since the war first broke out following joint US-Israeli strikes in February.

Saudi Arabia, Qatar and United Arab Emirates are among the US's Gulf allies that have been hit by Iranian strikes over the course of the war, in addition to threat of strikes that have led to major air travel disruptions in the region.
This is not the first time that Trump has said Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now.
Trump has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President Vance blamed on the Iran War.
In an interview with 60 minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the war.
Ahead of the midterms, Trump said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Post-election recriminations over the US war in Iran are already placing pressure on members of the Trump administration.

Republican congressman Thomas Massie launched a strong attack against Trump's Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over the war in Iran, requesting a vote in the House of Representatives to impeach him.
Trump has backed Hegseth, who says he is "not worried" about the looming impeachment threats, calling Massie's effort a "sham".

While the move is unlikely to succeed with Republicans still in control of Congress until January, Democrats have expressed willingness to impeach Hegseth once the new session begins and they have control of both the House and the Senate.

articles.title: Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most roles moving to India
articles.summary: The Australian airline said the move was aimed at modernising its IT systems and noted the impact of AI.

blocks.text: Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to consulting giant Accenture with most roles moving to India as the airline fast-tracks AI investment.
In an internal email to staff on Tuesday, the Australian company's CEO Vanessa Hudson said "this is hard news for some and I'm sorry for the uncertainty it brings".

The job cuts will begin mid-2027, she said, and start with finance, procurement, people and marketing roles shifting "mostly" to teams in India and "some in Australia" as the firm seeks to modernise its IT systems.
Hudson said the "scale and speed of change in technology and AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime", and it was in talks with unions and staff on the plans.
The move comes days after the airline provided a market update, flagging fare increases and flight cuts amid higher fuel costs.
On its new multi-year deal with Accenture, Hudson said it was about "modernising" the airline's IT systems to become "more efficient".
Qantas spends more than AU$1bn (US$691m; £514m) a year on technology, she said, and the company's back-end systems needed to be upgraded.
"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," she said.

The deal with Accenture means "we will redesign and simplify parts of how our corporate functions work and reduce duplication", Hudson said, so staff can "spend more time on work that creates value for our customers and the business".
The company said that "in time", the work that Accenture takes over will be "transformed further with automation and AI".
Staff affected by the job cuts will be redeployed "where possible", the firm added, including new roles in Australia.
Qantas - which employs about 28,000 staff in Australia and another 4,000 globally - said thousands of its staff already use AI in their daily work.
The BBC has contacted the Australian Services Union for comment.

articles.title: 'Cruise for life' ship seized in Singapore
articles.summary: The ship was meant to take guests around the world, but the trip was cut short after its operator ran out of money.

blocks.text: A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore.
The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024 and was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, is now anchored in Singapore port waters, local authorities say.

Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".
The crew onboard are reported to be well, Singapore's port authority said.
"Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," the authority said, adding that the vessel had been "placed under arrest pursuant to a court order".
Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.
The Odyssey was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.

Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.
Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 (£89,272) to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month, according to its website.
"For roughly the price of a car, you can own your home on a ship that travels the world," its founder Mikael Petterson had earlier said.
However the cruise was beset with problems from the start, with its departure delayed for four months because of repairs and paperwork.

While in Vietnam, crew members reportedly bought food from local grocery stores because the company owed money to a vendor who refused to deliver food, according to CBS News, the BBC's partner in the US.

CBS also reported that the operator warned passengers of its financial troubles in August, when it had sailed on a separate occasion into Singapore, and had to raise money from guests to keep the cruise going.
It had also mentioned the risk of being detained then.
Holly Hennessey, one of the ship's passengers, had earlier told the BBC guests were asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".
The vessel sailed again into Singapore earlier this month, weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end while in Cambodia.

As the Iran war sent fuel prices soaring earlier this year, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on 27 October.
It added that it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption" but those measures turned out to be insufficient to offset the "extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
The company also said it was working with residents to "identify temporary living arrangements" while in Cambodia.

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon denies being ‘obsessed’ with Jesse Baird as evidence to double murder trial continues
articles.summary:
Former police officer tells jury he joked about being ‘white girl crazy’ with friends as lawyer questions him over start of relationship with Baird

Beau Lamarre-Condon has denied being…

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon has denied being “obsessed” with Jesse Baird from the start of their relationship, telling a court he would have liked the TV presenter even if he was “a garbage cleaner”.
The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Sitting in the witness box for the fourth day, Lamarre-Condon was grilled by crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC about his relationship with Baird.
The former officer told the NSW supreme court he would meet up with Baird in October and November 2022 for sexual encounters before the pair began going on romantic dates in December of that year.
Under cross-examination on Tuesday, Hatfield asked Lamarre-Condon: “You were obsessed with him right from the start?”
Lamarre-Condon denied this, telling the jury: “I never cared about showing Jesse off. I wanted Jesse to meet my friends because I thought he was genuine”.
“Jesse Baird could have been a garbage cleaner… I liked Jesse for who he was as a person,” Lamarre-Condon said.
Asked by Hatfield if Lamarre-Condon was “obsessed” with Baird in February and March 2023, the accused responded: “I don’t agree with ‘obsessed’. Smitten? Yes. Obsessed? no.”

blocks.caption: Supplied images of Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird (right). Composite: Supplied/NSW Supreme Court

blocks.text: Hatfield pointed to messages between Lamarre-Condon and his friends sent around the time the pair began going on dates, where the officer says: “it sounds crazy, I love him”.
Lamarre-Condon responded: “I say ‘I love you’ to all my friends and to people like that all the time.”
“That’s different to saying I’m ‘in’ love with him,” he said.

Asked whether he was insecure about the relationship and whether Baird liked him, Lamarre-Condon said his response was “natural” and sometimes occurred when the TV presenter did not reply to his messages straight away.
“I would always joke [with my friends], ‘we’re white girl crazy’,” Lamarre-Condon told the jury.
“It means we should stop being in our head and second-guessing ourselves.”
He told the court he would make jokes and have “banter” with his female friends, not his heterosexual male friends, telling each other things like: “you’re a crazy bitch”.
Hatfield showed screenshots of text messages between Baird and Lamarre-Condon and asked why Baird’s profile photo were low resolution.
“If you’re trying to insinuate any of these are not genuine … we’ve got videos,” the officer said, telling the court Baird’s photo was a screenshot from a video he took of the presenter.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: Epstein associate who still runs model agency 'put me in danger' says abuse survivor
articles.summary: A woman says an agency boss sent her to photoshoots at the sex offender's Florida beach home.
articles.byline: Oana Marocico, Sheida Kiran, Haya Al Badarneh

blocks.text: A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the convicted sex offender's Florida beach house.
At the time, in 2009, Epstein was serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was allowed to work each day from his home.
"My agency's job was to protect me, and they failed. In fact, they put me in danger. And for that, they should be held accountable," she tells the BBC World Service.

Roza was 18 when she was first sent to Epstein's Palm Beach home by MC2 Model Management's US branch, having only arrived in the US from Uzbekistan about a month earlier. MC2's US president at the time, Jeff Fuller, now runs another US model agency called The Source Models.
"My agency knew exactly where I was. So Jeff knew exactly where I was going," says Roza.

She shows us an expense statement suggesting Fuller himself booked her flight home from Palm Beach, following her second shoot at Epstein's home. Fuller has previously claimed he did not know Roza was going to Epstein's house.

She says the photoshoots led to her being employed as an assistant to Epstein. Other survivors have explained how the financier used the recruitment of assistants as an elaborate ruse to allow him to continue abusing young women.
Roza says Epstein went on to systematically rape her.
Fuller has not responded to the BBC's allegations. He has previously said he did not know Roza was being abused.
We discovered through the Epstein-related documents released by the US Department of Justice [DOJ] that 10 models from MC2 met, or were in communication with, Epstein after his conviction.
The files also show Epstein gave $1m (£742,000) to MC2 in 2005 - despite the agency owners telling a US publication two years later that Epstein had no involvement in their company.

Testimony shared with BBC Eye also raises questions about the role played by two other individuals who were active in the model industry, and whom the DOJ files show had close relationships with Epstein - former agent Ramsey Elkholy and agency director Faith Kates.

A DOJ statement from last year, that no evidence has been uncovered which would warrant further investigation against "uncharged third parties", is now being challenged by New York State senator, Zellnor Myrie.
He has proposed a new sex trafficking bill to give police greater power to investigate Epstein's alleged enablers.
If you are outside the UK, please watch on YouTube, external
An email in the DOJ files, from Fuller to Epstein, makes clear the close ties between the agency and the financier.
"Had it not been for you, we would have fired her months ago," Fuller writes of another model in March 2012. "And I would be careful as she blabs about things," he says.

A month after Epstein's second arrest in 2019, MC2's US branch was dissolved and Fuller opened a new agency, The Source Models, which is still operating. The BBC has found that 50 models from MC2 were transferred to his new agency.
We asked The Source Models to comment on our findings - it did not reply.
Model agencies were useful to Epstein, says Sigrid McCawley, the lead lawyer for more than 100 of Epstein's victims.

"Epstein said to many people he wanted three different girls a day. Think about those numbers... The [model] scouts were really critical because they were the ones who were identifying the type of woman that Epstein liked."
In the case of former agent Ramsey Elkholy, BBC Eye has discovered he tried to connect 34 women to Epstein, including an 18-year-old who was still in school.
The experience of one of the women highlights how assistants would be co-opted into the structure of the abuse.
Elkholy, the DOJ files show, suggested to Epstein that one of the financier's female assistants befriend this woman, before introducing her to Epstein.
We spoke to this woman, and she revealed that at her first meeting with Epstein, aged 19, he sexually abused her in his New York townhouse.

Ramsey Elkholy told the BBC: "I completely reject any allegation that I knew of or facilitated abuse of any kind… At the time, I had no knowledge of any abuse and I knew only his own [Epstein's] account of his 2008 [legal] case, which I misguidedly believed."

He continued: "The record and published reporting show that women were often groomed by other women in his inner circle. I was never part of that circle, or indeed of any such activity… my intention was to help models find professional opportunities by introducing them to an extremely well-connected individual."

items: If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence, information and support is available at BBC Action Line

blocks.text: Lawyer Sigrid McCawley says these female assistants would have had "no choice" in how they conducted themselves.
"These young survivors were being abused regularly. Their livelihoods were being threatened… They had to do what they were being told to do."
Another model we have spoken to, Simona (not her real name), from eastern Europe, told us Epstein had raped her more than 200 times.
"People think that we gained something, that we agreed on this abuse in order to gain something, whether it's monetary or influential, but it's not true. We're left with deep trauma," says Simona.
She says the first time she met the financier, aged 20, she was already signed with a model agency in New York, and he offered to introduce her to his "good" friend Faith Kates.

At the time, Kates was the head of Next Management, one of the world's biggest model agencies. She stepped down from that senior executive position in December last year, but is still legally listed as a director of the company.
Simona says at this meeting, Kates suggested she undergo plastic surgery and sent details of a surgeon to Epstein.
After her meeting with Kates, Simona says Epstein convinced her to stop modelling.
And just like Roza, and several other of his victims, she became his assistant. She says he went on to rape her and control every aspect of her life for nearly two years.
The DOJ files show Epstein asked Kates to meet an additional five models, though it is not clear how many of these meetings took place.

Lawyers for Faith Kates told the BBC: "Jeffrey Epstein was a master manipulator... Ms Kates was one of those grossly misled by Epstein. Had she known then what she - and everyone else - now knows, she would have never associated with him."
They added she had never asked a model to have plastic surgery.
We approached Next Management for comment, but it did not reply.

Myrie told the BBC that if his bill were to become law, and "you were sending models to Epstein and you knew what Epstein was doing, or you should have known what he was doing, you will be held accountable".
Roza hopes sharing her story will encourage others to come forward.
"There are many, many survivors out there who never speak, because it's scary. So to all my sister survivors… you know me now. You know my name. I say, reach out."
Additional reporting by Annika Grosser

articles.title: Ukraine peace talks resume with 'some flexibility' by warring sides, US officials say
articles.summary: Kyiv, Washington and Moscow are all sending delegation to the United Arab Emirates for the first trilateral talks since February.

blocks.text: Moscow and Kyiv are privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would controls Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario, US officials have said.
The comments came on the eve of the first trilateral talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine since February.
Senior officials from Moscow, Kyiv and Washington will meet in Abu Dhabi as the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches.

Jared Kushner - Donald Trump's son-in-law and part of the US delegation alongside peace envoy Steve Witkoff - said the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.
"An important part of this process is encouraging all parties to begin thinking seriously about what comes after the war," Kushner wrote on X.
But Moscow and Kyiv's positions on ending the conflict in the first place remain far apart.
A key area of disagreement between the two involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is by now mostly occupied by Russia.

Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk which it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those sections, which it says are crucial to its future security.

While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".
However, he acknowledged that the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture".

"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."

For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it's attacked again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from eastern Europe – which would be alarming to Europeans.

The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.

The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since.

Since then, European leaders - who have been largely excluded from peace talks – have pushed to be involved in the process amid concerns that decisions about the security of their continent would be made without them.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged on Monday to include Nato allies and EU members into any "meaningful discussions about Europe's security architecture". President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly stated Kyiv wanted Europe to be part of the talks.

The US official said the Americans would propose moving into a multilateral format bringing the Europeans into the discussion. "Hopefully we'll get the Russians on board," the official said, while acknowledging that "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans."

Since the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump – who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day – has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success.
Meanwhile, his increasingly conciliatory approach towards Moscow has fuelled deep unease in Kyiv and across the European Union.
After meeting Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev in Washington last week, Trump touted a forthcoming "big, beautiful agreement" on Ukraine which "might involve all of Europe".
Many in Ukraine are sceptical that this would result into a fair peace.

Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the foreign affairs parliamentary committee, told the BBC he believes Trump wants "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", which will certainly be rejected by Kyiv.
The only way to make Putin start real negotiations is by putting greater pressure on Russia through sanctions and deep strikes, Merezhko said.

"While Putin has a war machine up and running, he has no incentives to negotiate." He also mentioned recent moves by Trump, such as his deal to buy diesel from Russia, as something that "only encourages Moscow to continue the war".
Moscow's delegation in Abu Dhabi will include Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yury Zhigarlovsky.

Kyiv is sending several senior officials who have been part of previous negotiating teams, including Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, and MP Davyd Arakhamiya.

Away from Abu Dhabi, Russia continues to pummel Ukraine with deadly bombardments and strikes on energy infrastructure, viewed in Kyiv as proof Moscow wants to corner Ukraine into accepting a deal on Russia's terms.
On Monday, Kushner was cautious to point out that the Abu Dhabi talks could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations."
"This is an extraordinarily difficult and complicated conflict," he wrote on X, adding the US was "approaching these discussions with determination and realism."

articles.title: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
articles.summary: A tug-of-war between China and the US could have a big impact on energy costs, but who will win?

blocks.text: A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.
In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.
For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.
Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.
Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.

And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK.

As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.

America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.
Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.

The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills?
Two decisions

On the Moray Firth near Inverness, a long spit of sand and dunes curls out into the sea at Whiteness Head. Behind it lies a yard where, for nearly 30 years, thousands of workers built the giant platforms that opened up North Sea oil.

Ming Yang, one of China's biggest wind turbine makers, wanted to bring it back to life with a £1.5bn factory and up to 1,500 jobs initially generated. In March, after US lawmakers had urged the UK to block it, ministers did just that, citing national security.
Panorama, Fire and Floods: Our Extreme Weather
9 November 2026
Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw. No to Chinese wind turbines; yes to North Sea gas.

Few countries are more exposed to the energy shock than the UK. Gas heats most homes and, much of the time, sets the wholesale price of electricity. The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra £63bn – around £2,200 each – according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Wind turbines represent homegrown energy, but they come with potential problems

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Wind turbines represent homegrown energy, but they come with potential problems
Less than half of the UK's gas now comes from its own North Sea fields, and the energy we import often comes from places that turn out to be unstable or unreliable.

At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama.
But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt."
"We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy."
There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it.
The case for drilling

Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!"
Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field.

Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fahnbulleh, centre, at Jackdaw last month. She says the drilling will have minimal impact on energy prices

blocks.text: Image source, Press Association
Fahnbulleh, centre, at Jackdaw last month. She says the drilling will have minimal impact on energy prices

The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills".
"If we use our own gas… that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice.
Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress.
But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets."

Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had."

Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year – even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead.

Whatever ministers decide, the basin's most productive days are behind it. Jackdaw's reserves amount to only a few months of UK gas demand, while Rosebank contains less than a year's worth of our oil consumption.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The debate around Rosebank and Jackdaw has sparked vehement opposition from climate protesters

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The debate around Rosebank and Jackdaw has sparked vehement opposition from climate protesters

And last week the government introduced a bill to write its ban on new exploration licences into law. Rosebank, which is already licensed, is not covered. That could let ministers have it both ways: approve the last big field, while promising there will never be another.
With bills set to rise again in January, that may prove a tempting combination.
The case for electrons
The alternative is to build.
Gas is bought, burned and bought again. A wind turbine or solar panel costs money to put up but can then generate electricity for decades without needing shipments of fuel.

The government's climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee, calculate that a future price shock like 2022's would push household energy bills up 59% if Britain stayed on a high-carbon path - but only 4% if it focused on renewables.

The cost of power from new solar farms fell by 90% between 2010 and 2024, and from onshore wind by 70%, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. But the recent bout of global inflation has been pushing initial costs back up. Last year the Danish developer Ørsted scrapped plans for Hornsea 4, a giant wind farm off the Yorkshire coast, blaming soaring supply chain costs.
Higher interest rates have made things worse. Most of the cost of a wind or solar farm comes up front, so developers must borrow heavily before they generate any power.

And there is another problem. Britain needs expensive new electricity networks to bring that renewable power to the towns and cities where it is needed. Meanwhile, gas-fired stations still frequently set wholesale power prices - meaning any cost savings are not always reflected in customer bills.
All of which means building more renewables does not automatically mean lower household bills.
The China question
And there is another issue - China's dominance of clean tech. It makes the vast majority of the world's solar panels and batteries, and around two-thirds of its electric cars.
And China's lead is growing. In March, its exports of solar panels, batteries and electric cars hit a record, up 70% on a year earlier, according to the think tank Ember.

The UK wants to escape the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price shocks and keep adding to global warming. Much of the technology needed to replace those fuels comes from China - a country it is increasingly reluctant to depend on.
I asked Fahnbulleh whether Britain was swapping dependence on petrostates for dependence on Beijing. "Well, look, we are," she said, adding: "we've got a diversified global market".
Britain will keep buying from China where it needs to, says Fahnbulleh, but she wants more of the kit made here. "I want to see turbines," she said.
Yet UK-built turbines were exactly what Ming Yang was offering.
"There was a security risk, and national security comes first and foremost," says Fahnbulleh. The government has never publicly explained what that risk was.
Two days before Jackdaw was approved, Japan's Sumitomo Electric opened Britain's first HVDC subsea cable factory at Nigg, a short way up the coast from Whiteness Head, creating up to 250 jobs.
Foreign investment, then - just not from China.
Role reversal

Earlier this year the US formally left the Paris climate agreement and is not expected to send a delegation to this year's COP. Without American pressure, others have less reason to make bold promises: national pledges now add up to a cut in global emissions of just 6% by 2035, the UN says – a tenth of what scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5C.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Donald Trump is a big exponent of fossil fuels

blocks.text: Donald Trump is a big exponent of fossil fuels

China is beginning to fill the space. Li Shuo, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, calls it a "role reversal". Once "a very conservative player" at climate talks, China now sees pushing the global climate agenda as serving its national interest – and, he says, "we're only at the beginning of this". It aims to hit one of COP31's flagship goals, getting 35% of its energy from electricity, five years early.
And increasingly it is Chinese companies, rather than governments' promises, that are driving the transition. "It's really just a China story," says Li Shuo.
If that is right, it leaves the UK in an uncomfortable place. Hard choices – and they come when household budgets are already stretched thin.

articles.title: New trilateral talks on Ukraine war in Abu Dhabi: What to expect?
articles.summary: Ukrainian and Russian representatives last met in February for talks on ending the war, but the same sticking points remain. Ukraine continues to demand security guarantees, which is a non-starter…

blocks.text: A new round of trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States are scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, months after a flurry of US-mediated peace talks earlier this year in January and February went nowhere.

When announcing the new trilateral talks last week, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said the discussions would focus on "post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has named security guarantees, an energy ceasefire, unblocking the Black Sea, extended prisoner exchanges, and preparations for a meeting of the leaders of Ukraine, the United States and Russia as his key topics.
Lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia, a member of Ukraine's delegation, told DW he was not expecting quick progress.

"I don't think there will be a breakthrough, after there was such a long break in the negotiation process," he said. "Simply the fact that trilateral talks are being resumed can be counted as a success."
Who is sitting at the table?
Witkoff will be joined by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, real estate developer Jared Kushner, who serves as special envoy.

The Kremlin has sent Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, to act as chief negotiator, along with a delegation including high-ranking Russian military and intelligence officials.
The Ukrainian delegation will be led by Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, along with Arakhamia, and diplomatic and military officials.
Europe joins in
Separate formats are planned with several European representatives.

These include Günter Sautter, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's foreign and security policy adviser, Emmanuel Bonne, head of the Elysee Palace's diplomatic service and Jonathan Powell, the UK's national security advisor, and Fabrizio Saggio, diplomatic adviser to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
Björn Seibert, Chief of Staff for the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and Geoffrey van Leeuwen, Chief of Staff for NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, will also attend.
It's doubtful, however, whether European representatives will be formally involved in talks on a potential peace deal.
Hanna Shelest, a security studies director at the foreign policy network Ukrainian Prism, told DW she believed they'd play "an observing role, at best."

She added that, until now, Russia had been reluctant to have European representatives at the table to uphold the impression that talks were "a matter between two superpowers" — namely, Russia and the United States — and to increase pressure on Washington.
"I doubt the Russian delegation will let the Europeans have a say," she told DW.

"Experience from the past years has taught us that as soon as Medinsky heads negotiations, the point becomes demonstrating to the US that Russia is willing to talk, but in reality, they won't reach an agreement," she explained. "Instead, there will be a long sermon about history and all sorts of other things."
However, she said Moscow sending high-ranking intelligence officers as part of the delegation was a "fairly positive aspect" of Russia's intentions.
She believed that additional negotiations were possible at this level.

This could include over prisoner exchanges or humanitarian pauses in villages near Oleshky, a town in the Russian occupied Kherson region in Ukraine's south, where US First Lady Melania Trump was credited with arranging a temporary truce in late October that secured humanitarian aid and allowed civilians to evacuate.
But despite these "positive signals," Shelest cautioned against hoping for concrete results, and suspected Russia was using the talks to stall.
Oleshky truce as a template for wider ceasefire?
Late last week, Trump spoke of a "big beautiful agreement," after speaking with Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, "that might involve all of Europe."

This new security architecture, Kushner later clarified on social media, would be centered around "permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability."
These points "don't contain anything the Russians haven't been talking about since 2009," Shelest said.

Ivan Us, chief consultant and economic diplomacy expert at Ukraine's National Institute for Strategic Studies, pointed out that negotiations with people who are not decisions-makers could be simply for show.
But he agreed with other expert observers that negotiators in Abu Dhabi might try to use the temporary truce brokered for Oleshky as a model for other limited humanitarian ceasefires in the region.
But while Us said he saw cause for optimism, he also cautioned that Russia had continued attacks in Ukraine during the Oleshky truce, and had used the pause to fortify its positions around the town.
This article originally appeared in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Trump says Nvidia boss told him he had no idea woman he had affair with was Chinese spy
articles.summary: The US president said the FBI is now investigating the affair. He said he spoke with Jensen Huang and asked him about the affair.

blocks.text: Donald Trump has said the boss of Nvidia, whose affair with an alleged Chinese spy is being investigated, told him that he had "no idea she was a spy".
The US President said he spoke with CEO Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.
"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Trump said the FBI was also investigating the affair. China has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia, who commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
Trump said the FBI was also investigating the affair but did not elaborate on the probe or when it was launched.
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.

articles.title: Canadian ultramarathoner Stephanie Case is the 1st woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica
articles.summary: Canadian ultramarathoner Stephanie Case completed the Antarctic Ice Ultra in Queen Maud Land, Eastern Antarctica, on Sunday, making her the first woman to run 100 miles, or 160.9 kilometres, on the…

image.caption: Stephanie Case, 44, at the finish line of the Antarctic Ice Ultra on Sunday in Queen Maud Land, East Antarctica. She's now the first woman to run 100 miles on the icy continent. (Jan Lenfert/Peak Pixel Cafe/The North Face)

blocks.text: Canada

Canadian ultramarathoner Stephanie Case completed the Antarctic Ice Ultra in Queen Maud Land, Eastern Antarctica, on Sunday, making her the first woman to run 100 miles, or 160.9 kilometres, on the southernmost continent covered by the largest ice sheet in the world.
Case, 44, crossed the line in 17 hours, 31 minutes and 39 seconds
She admits the race — in which she ran a 4.2 kilometre loop 38 times over 17 hours on the coldest and windiest continent on the planet — had her rethinking her life choices at times.

But Canadian ultramarathoner Stephanie Case still bested the Antarctic Ice Ultra in Queen Maud Land, Eastern Antarctica, on Sunday. That makes her the first woman to run 100 miles, or 160.9 kilometres, on the southernmost continent covered by the largest ice sheet in the world.
She carried a Canadian flag and cried happy tears as she crossed the finish line in 17:31:39. Her running shoes crunched and squeaked through the frigid packed snow.
"I knew roughly what I would be facing, but I had never experienced an environment as extreme as that before," Case, 44, told CBC News Monday.
"It feels pretty amazing to put women on the map there, especially in a place that used to be called the womanless continent."
Organizers call it the "ultimate test of human endurance at the bottom of the world." Runners have been braving icy temperatures in the Antarctic Ice Ultra since its inaugural race in 2024.
For safety reasons, the course is a 4.2-kilometre looped circuit around a basecamp — meaning those who completed the 100-mile ultramarathon ran the same loop 38 times plus another 300 metres.
Stephanie Case during the Antarctic Ice Ultra on Sunday. (Jan Lenfert/Peak Pixel Cafe/The North Face)

Case says she got into a rhythm, focusing on 10 loops at a time to make it a full marathon before stopping to warm up in the aid tent. Although on the first round, she had to stop after eight loops because her balaclava had iced up so much she couldn't breathe through it.
They also had to start racing at 1 a.m., the coldest part of the night, due to incoming storms, Case said.

Race organizers described Case's time as "blazing fast" in an Instagram post, adding it was "an extraordinary display of speed, strength and endurance in one of the most extreme environments on Earth."
She placed second overall out of 28 runners. Yusheng Ni of China won the race, finishing in 17:02:24.
Stephanie Case just after crossing the finish line. (Jan Lenfert/Peak Pixel Cafe/The North Face)
'Motherhood isn't the finish line'
This isn't the first time Case, 44, a former UN human rights lawyer who was born in Kingston, Ont., has made global headlines for smashing gruelling races.

In May 2025, Case won the Ultra-Trail Snowdonia in Wales, where she placed first among women with a time of 16:53:22 and went viral for the race photos where she breastfeeds her daughter, Pepper, who was six months old at the time.
Some of the attention was negative, Case says, explaining there were people who said she should be at home with her baby, and that she was selfish for training with a young daughter.

items: Canadian wins 100-km ultramarathon while stopping to breastfeed her baby along the way
A runner died in the New York City Marathon. Have the risks changed as more people race?

blocks.text: "I think that is completely the wrong narrative," Case said.
"Moms shouldn't feel guilty for prioritizing things that make them feel happy and whole — it makes us better parents in the end."
Ultrarunner Stephanie Case is pictured during the Ultra-Trail Snowdonia in Wales, where she came in first, on May 17, 2025. (Stephanie Case)
Now, Case says she's excited to go home to Chamonix, France, and tell Pepper all about her race. Pepper also watched her finish on the livestream, she added.
"I hope this shows everyone that motherhood isn't the finish line," she said.
"I was racing to prove to myself, and to anyone out there, that moms can do pretty badass things."

Next up for Case is the Arctic Spine, a 472-kilometre trail race in northern Sweden in February. She noted she will need to go on skis, pull her own sled, melt her own snow and pitch her own tent. And she joked that the extreme conditions in the Antarctic Race Ultra had her questioning her decision to sign up for her upcoming expedition through the Arctic tundra.
"I was rethinking my life choices out there during the race in Antarctica, I must say."
Stephanie Case pictured during the the Antarctic Ice Ultra on Sunday. (Antarctica Ice Ultra/Runbuk)
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: A surprise baby right whale spotted near Quebec is bringing 'a lot of hope' for the species
articles.summary: Scientists were shocked and delighted to discover a previously unaccounted for baby right whale swimming alongside its mama off the coast of Quebec.

image.caption: This photo provided by the Mingan Island Cetacean Study shows a North Atlantic Right whale mother, Silt, with her calf in the Jacques-Cartier Passage of the Gulf of St. Lawrence on Sept. 25. (Mathilde Laverdière/Mingan Island Cetacean Study/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: As It Happens
Scientists were shocked and delighted to discover a previously unaccounted for baby right whale swimming alongside its mama off the coast of Quebec.
This is the most productive breeding season for the whales in 17 years
The surprisingly sneaky, 6,804-kilogram North Atlantic right whale calf had somehow evaded the watchful eyes of researchers who closely track endangered species' population
That is, until it was photographed in September off Anticosti Island.
"To be completely honest, I was a bit skeptical at first," Amy Warren, scientist at the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center, told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.
But Warren and her colleagues painstakingly confirmed the discovery by identifying the mother and comparing the calf's distinctive markings to those of other whales already on file.

Its sudden appearance brings the number of baby right whales from the most recent birthing season to 24 — the most productive year for the species since 2009, and the fourth-highest count on record, the aquarium said.
"This year definitely brings a lot of hope and a lot of optimism," Warren said.
LISTEN | Interview with scientist Amy Warren:
As It Happens5:25Surprise baby right whale spotted near Quebec brings 'a lot of hope' for the species
Scientists who work with North Atlantic right whales don't always find a lot of reasons to be hopeful, says Warren.

There are only 380 in the world, according to the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and their population fell by 25 per cent between 2010 and 2020. There are only about 70 known reproductive-age females alive today.

That's, in part, because warming oceans are forcing the creatures away from protected areas and into places where they're extremely vulnerable to collisions with large ships and entanglement in commercial fishing gear

"It can be really hard work seeing these whales go through really traumatic events. We document their scars and their injuries, and we spend a lot of time talking about that and looking at that," Warren said.
"So to think about these calves and see these calves, and seeing so many of them, it's … really positive."
Trend or anomaly?

Things may be looking up. North Atlantic right whales have gained back some of their population since 2020, according to Fisheries and Oceans Canada, and this year's baby explosion has scientists cautiously optimistic.
But Warren says it's too soon to say whether this is part of an upward trend, or simply an anomaly.
"Maybe they have been finding better food sources, better food areas. That's quite possible," she said.
"We long to hope that some of the efforts that researchers and management are doing to protect them are also working. It's hard to say that, you know, with certainty."
'Did you see it?' Get a rare look at a North Atlantic right whale off N.L.
This newest calf belongs to a female known as Silt, who researchers say is at least 38 years old. This is her sixth calf.
"So she's a very well experienced mother," Warren said. "She last gave birth in 2022, so timing wise, this makes sense to be able to calf this year."
Right whales can technically give birth once every three years, though, in reality, Warren says they tend to wait between five and 10 years.
But that gap, she says, appears to be closing.
"Something we noticed with the females this year is that the average was closer to five years, when 10 years ago, it was the average of about 10 years between calves."
How did this calf stay hidden?

The elusive marine mammals give birth off the southeastern U.S. in winter before venturing north to New England and Canada to feed, and scientists keep a close eye on their population, photographing them extensively and cataloguing them based on their unique head markings.
The babies, Warren says, are hard to miss. They're still learning to swim and they can't hold their breath very long.
"Moms and calves spend a lot of time near the surface, which means they're more easily spotted," Warren said.

"So the fact that this mom calf pair managed to get likely from that area all the way up to Canada and almost back out without being spotted by any of the surveys along the way, it's quite impressive and quite rare."

items: North Atlantic right whales at greater risk of collision with boats at night: study
Internal DFO memo warns Trump-backed bill threatens right whale survival

blocks.text: The duo was sighted by researchers with Mingan Island Cetacean Study, a non-profit research organization in the province’s coastal Côte-Nord region.
“It just goes to show you how big the ocean is, and how those animals can get lost out there,” said Richard Sears, founder and director of Mingan Island Cetacean Study.
Warren, meanwhile, says she hopes it's a sign of a brighter future for North Atlantic right whales.
"That is the hope," she said. "But we will find out in the years to come."
With files from The Associated Press. Interview with Amy Warren produced by Leslie Amminson

articles.title: Trial date of alleged Charlie Kirk killer set for June 2028
articles.summary: Tyler Robinson has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the 2025 killing of the conservative activist.

blocks.text: The trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk, will start in June 2028, a judge has ordered.
Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the September 2025 killing of Kirk, 31, who was shot while he spoke at a Utah college campus.

Utah County judge Tony Graf Jr on Monday told the court that jury selection would begin on 21 June, 2028. The prosecution has estimated the trial could last 17 weeks, while defence lawyers have said it could take seven months.
Robinson could face the death penalty if found guilty of aggravated murder, something his defence team has sought to prevent.
Prosecutors previously told the court they could be ready for trial by October 2027 but were willing to move that date back to January 2028 to avoid the holiday period.

But defence attorneys said they needed more time to prepare their case and floated a 2029 start. As well as trying to stop Robinson facing the death penalty, they have also tried to have cameras banned from the courtroom.

Kirk's widow, Erika, with whom he had two children, had pushed for as early a trial date as possible while also arguing proceedings should be live-streamed. She, along with Kirk's parents, ⁠Robert and Kathryn, have attended a number of court hearings in the case.

At the end of Monday's proceedings, Erica Kirk's lawyer, Jeffrey A Nieman, told the judge that while "a trial in the summer of 2028, three years after Charlie's assassination, does not feel very speedy to the Kirk family", they had "no choice but obviously to accept the schedule the court's put forward".
Nieman added: "The family has waited long enough already; they should not have to wait any longer for this."
During a five-day preliminary hearing in July, prosecutors outlined their evidence to show probable cause for trial.

This included DNA allegedly tying Robinson to the murder weapon and other items recovered at the scene; confessions he allegedly made to loved ones; and a taped video statement from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs.
"There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court in September.

"We know that the defendant is the shooter… first, because of the video evidence; second, because of the DNA; third, because of his admissions; and fourth, because of circumstantial evidence," McBride said.
Defence attorneys, meanwhile, have cast doubt upon evidence and expert witness credentials in the case.

articles.title: Man who used fraudulent passport to get in and out of Canada 16 times handed 2-year sentence
articles.summary: A Ghanaian man who used a fraudulent Canadian passport to leave and re-enter the country 16 times has been sentenced to two years in prison for citizenship fraud.

image.caption: Jefferson Zormelo, 22, pleaded guilty earlier this year to violating the Canadian Citizenship Act by using a fraudulently issued passport to enter and exit the country 16 times. (Shutterstock)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
A Ghanaian man who used a fraudulent Canadian passport to leave and re-enter the country 16 times has been sentenced to two years in prison for citizenship fraud.
Jefferson Zormelo pleaded guilty to violating Canadian Citizenship Act
Jefferson Zormelo, 22, pleaded guilty earlier this year to violating the Canadian Citizenship Act.
On Monday in Calgary, Justice Karen Molle said Zormelo’s act “attacks the integrity of the Canadian citizenship regime.”
“The offence jeopardized public safety and our national security,” noted Molle. “Fraudulent use of Canadian passports affects Canada’s international reputation.”
With credit for the time he’s served since his arrest, Zormelo has about 14 months left behind bars.
Used airports in Montreal, Toronto, Halifax
Zormelo came to Canada on a study permit in 2021.

In 2024, when authorities determined he was no longer enrolled in school, an exclusion order was issued for his removal from the country, according to an agreed statement of facts filed as part of the guilty plea.

He then obtained identification documents, including a proof of citizenship under a false name, and used that to get a Canadian passport, which was issued under the name Mitchell Leblanc in December 2024.
Over the next 15 months, Zormelo then entered and exited Canada through Montreal's, Toronto's and Halifax’s international airports using the Leblanc passport a total of 16 times.
In April 2026, he was arrested by Canada Border Services Agency officers in Calgary after presenting a fake permanent residency card in the Leblanc name to officials at the U.S. Consulate.
Officers then searched Zormelo's hotel room and discovered, among other things, the fraudulent passport.
'Clever criminals pose a greater risk'
Prosecutor Tyler Lord had sought a five-year prison sentence.
Defence lawyer Devin Frank asked the court to consider a time-served sentence of nine months in jail, arguing his client experienced a difficult upbringing in Ghana, which involved poverty and abuse.
The judge noted Zormelo was "desperate to live and work in Canada."

items: Government abruptly suspends citizenship certificates issued under 'lost Canadians' law

blocks.text: In the end, Molle outlined a number of aggravating factors, including the fact that Zormelo used his intellect to commit the “sophisticated, elaborate” fraud.
“Clever criminals pose a greater risk to public safety,” said Molle.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Meghan Grant is a justice affairs reporter. She has been covering courts, crime and stories of police accountability in southern Alberta for more than 15 years. Send Meghan a story tip at meghan.grant@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case - media reports
articles.summary: The ruling means prosecutors can pursue the case, meaning they could reduce charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.

blocks.text: A Massachusetts judge has denied motions to dismiss the murder case of Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of murdering her three children, according to local US media.
The judge's ruling comes after Clancy's defence team requested dismissal of the case after her first trial ended in a mistrial in September, when a 12-person jury failed to reach a consensus.
The ruling clears the way for prosecutors to pursue the case. They could reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.
Clancy has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.
Clancy's defence team had filed three motions, including one to dismiss the case against her due to double jeopardy - a legal standard that says a person cannot be tried for the same crime twice.

Her lawyers argued that Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the August murder trial, acted prematurely when he declared a mistrial on 4 September, saying that he should have sought a viable alternative.
In his ruling on Monday, Sullivan said that a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject her to double jeopardy, according to Reuters news agency.
Sullivan also denied a motion to see records of the lone holdout juror in the case and to question the juror under oath.
The judge scheduled a hearing for 16 November to discuss when to hold a second trial. He has previously suggested it could begin in March.

articles.title: Witnesses recount struggle to save people buried in ‘horrifying’ Gaza landslide
articles.summary:
High winds and heavy train triggered collapse of sand bank overlooking camp for displaced families

Witnesses have described the frantic struggle to save three members of a family buried by a…
articles.byline: Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Jason Burke

blocks.text: Witnesses have described the frantic struggle to save three members of a family buried by a landslide triggered by high winds and heavy rain in Gaza.
A sand bank overlooking a camp for displaced families south of Deir al-Balah collapsed on Sunday, killing five people and crushing at least three tents.

“It was a horrifying sight,” said Abdul Karim al-Sahhar, 30, originally from Izbat Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza. “We saw people buried beneath the sand and rocks. None of them was moving or making a sound. Even the tent had disappeared completely. There was no trace of it left.”
Among the casualties was an eight-year-old, a six-year-old and their mother.

Sahhar, whose own shelter was badly damaged in the landslide, said the children’s father was outside the family tent and so survived. “One of his children had called him to come and eat with them,” he said. “He was a little late returning, and then the collapse happened.

“The father started shouting: ‘Save my children! Save my children!’ People came and started digging [but] there was a huge boulder on top of the victims. The young men had to break it into pieces so they could reach the people buried underneath.”

Abu Darbali, another witness, said the collapse of the embankment sounded like an explosion. “We found that three tents were covered completely after the mountain collapsed on top of them,” he told Reuters. “People were under the rubble and we couldn’t see them.”
Video posted to social media showed residents using hammers to break large rocks and others removing sand with shovels, searching for people trapped underneath using flashlights.

blocks.caption: Palestinians remove sand at the site of the deadly sand bank collapse. Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/Reuters

blocks.text: The UN said more than 26,000 households had reported damage to shelters or belongings after the weekend’s rainstorms.

The vast majority of Gaza’s population of 2.3 million live in tent encampments or the ruins of bombed-out buildings, ‌with reconstruction yet to begin after Israel’s relentless two-year military assault launched after the Hamas attacks on southern Israel in October 2023.

“The collapse [this weekend] was waiting to happen. [Gaza] is extremely overcrowded. People are just trying to find a place wherever,” said Toby Fricker, a spokesperson for Unicef, which has been working to prevent similar tragedies and improve drainage in camps for the displaced.

In a statement, the Hamas-run government media office said about “70,000 tents sheltering tens of thousands of displaced people were flooded on the first day” of rains. It also noted the “collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs, which caused injuries”, some critical, in various areas of the tiny territory.

A US-brokered ceasefire last year called for the eventual reconstruction of Gaza, but little progress has been made. Negotiators have failed to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm or for Israel to withdraw its troops, which control about two-thirds of the territory ‌from which residents have been ordered to leave.
Israel says no reconstruction can happen before Hamas is disarmed.

Sahhar said he and his family were now homeless. “My tent and everything I own are now buried under the sand. My mattress, household utensils and all my belongings – everything was buried. I could not retrieve anything,” he said.

blocks.caption: Palestinians inspect tents buried under rocks following the collapse of a large sandstone slab. Photograph: Abdel Kareem Hana/AP

blocks.text: Mustafa Qazzaat, a member of the Gaza City council, said Israel had not allowed prefabricated homes to shelter the displaced since the truce was announced, and only permitted the entry of limited numbers of tents.
Many so-called “dual use” items remain restricted, such as metal tent poles. Humanitarian workers said they instead had used wooden poles fashioned from palettes used to transport food.

Cogat, the Israeli defence ministry body that oversees aid to Gaza, said over 91,000 tents and over 8,200 trucks containing tarpaulins, blankets and winter clothinghad reached Gaza, as well as convoys carrying supplies of fuel and engine oil to power pumping facilities and other humanitarian installations.

Earlier this year, an assessment compiled by shelter specialists in Gaza revealed that thousands of tents supplied by China, Egypt and Saudi Arabia to shelter displaced Palestinians offered only limited protection against rain and wind.

articles.title: Russia's leading independent newspaper closes after eviction
articles.summary: The outlet has been evicted from its offices of three decades and says it's been blocked from receiving donations.

blocks.text: Russia's leading independent newspaper has closed after being evicted from its offices and facing pressure from authorities.
For 30 years, Novaya Gazeta published investigations into corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power in the country.
On Monday, the team behind the newspaper had a final editorial meeting before packing up their belongings and leaving.
The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia's media was highly diverse and that the newspaper's closure was part of "a standard rotational process".
The BBC spoke to its co-founder Dmitry Muratov, a Nobel Peace Prize winner, about the closure.

articles.title: Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 16 people
articles.summary: Eyewitnesses say the explosion shook the ground, with one believing an earthquake had hit near the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga.
